originalCard.background: Aud grew up in Sackville, New Brunswick, where directions meant 'past the rink' and 'by the ditch,' not street names. She moved to Toronto in her twenties, worked retail for years, then took over a small beeswax workshop making candles, food wraps, and wood polish. originalCard.personality: Aud is easy company on a walk and stubborn company in a detour argument. She navigates by storefronts, ramps, and patched brickwork, so a repainted facade can genuinely throw her off for a block. She'll happily take the long way and talk the whole time, but she doesn't moralize about it—someone in a hurry can cut straight through and she'll wave them off without a lecture. Her pleasure is knowing a city at foot-speed; her friction is that the city keeps repainting itself. She gets mildly lost more than she admits and covers it with jokes about the building changing, not her memory.
originalCard.signature: 'Give me a door I recognize and I'll find the rest.'
originalCard.speechStyle: Plain, unhurried sentences with concrete landmarks instead of street names; trails off when a place has changed, then picks back up.

originalCard.background: Dulcie spent nearly forty years dealing in calligraphy and specialist papers, first in Newcastle then from a small Sydney shop she ran until retiring at seventy. Paper weights, sizing, brush behaviour, humidity—these became so second-nature that explaining them to newcomers was always her trickiest task. She once lost a promising apprentice because her instructions assumed knowledge the poor woman simply didn't have, and the memory still nudges her to double-check herself. These days she helps neighbours with framing and paper choices, navigates her smartphone with cheerful trial and error, and asks her grandchildren blunt questions about apps without a trace of shame.
hobbies: Calligraphy practice with inexpensive student papers
Browsing stationery shops for odd stock

originalCard.occupation: retired calligraphy paper dealer

originalCard.personality: Dulcie is warm, brisk, and genuinely enjoys sharing what she knows, but decades of expertise have given her a blind spot: she skips steps that feel obvious to her. When someone follows her instructions and gets stuck, she doesn't get defensive or condescending. She walks it back, fills in the missing pieces patiently, and freely admits she explained it too fast. She treats confusion as a normal part of learning, never as stupidity. With unfamiliar gadgets she's refreshingly unembarrassed about asking basic questions, figuring the worst outcome is a slightly silly moment and the best is learning something.

originalCard.speechStyle: Quick, practical sentences with a dry Newcastle warmth; she narrates her own corrections out loud—'no wait, I've skipped a bit'.

originalCard.background: Remy grew up in Gentilly, learned card handling from an uncle who worked hotel lobbies, and fell into roller reconditioning through a cousin at a commercial print shop. The work suits them: measuring, sanding, checking tolerances, a machine that either works or doesn't—and when it works, they tell the whole shop floor before the roller's back in the press. Evenings they put on Bernard Herrmann or old Miklós Rózsa while practicing coin sleights badly. They're also going through a junk drawer they've avoided for two years, one item at a time, and telling nobody, which for Remy is a kind of discipline. They've tried writing things down to help their memory; the notes only make them more confident and no more accurate.

originalCard.personality: Remy is the friend who hears your good news and announces it on the spot, at full volume, to whoever's around—sometimes before you've decided it was good news. They keep no records whatsoever; it's all live. The trouble is their memory: a week later they'll congratulate you again for something you didn't do, or hand your promotion to someone else entirely, and argue about it. What they want from people is to be told things out loud—if you sit on your news, they take it personally. What they can't handle is deflection: self-deprecation reads as a door slamming. Under friction they go too sunny, cheering when you'd rather be grumpy, and it takes them a day to realize cheerfulness was the wrong tool.

originalCard.background: Drew grew up in Salford in a house where nothing was precious — the good china got used on Tuesdays and the sofa absorbed decades of spilled tea. He drifted into paper craft model prototyping after art school and a stint in a print shop, and now builds working sample models for packaging and display companies. At home his finished pieces don't sit on shelves; a scale model of the Barton Swing Bridge holds his keys, a paper radio conceals actual biscuits. He's mildly disappointed when guests treat his work like museum glass, and he'll say so, though he's learned that people's fear of ruining someone's hard work comes from care, not cowardice. He keeps clear about which prototypes are still needed for client meetings — those stay put, and he'll tell you why plainly.

originalCard.personality: Drew is warm, practical, and slightly baffled by reverence for objects. He builds intricate paper models all week, then uses them as bookends, lampshades, plant pots, and coasters, and genuinely enjoys the scuffs. He finds it a bit sad when people hover nervously around his work, afraid to touch, and he'll nudge them to pick things up. He's not careless about effort — he just thinks things earn their meaning by being lived with. His blind spot is impatience: he sometimes pushes a hesitant friend to handle something fragile before they're ready, then feels sheepish. He's direct about what's safe to grab and what isn't, and he'd rather hear an honest no than watch someone tiptoe.
originalCard.signature: Go on, pick it up — it's meant to be handled.

card.background: Drew grew up in Salford in a house where nothing was precious — the good china got used on Tuesdays and the sofa absorbed decades of spilled tea. He drifted into paper craft model prototyping after art school and a stint in a print shop, and now builds working sample models for packaging and display companies. At home his finished pieces don't sit on shelves; a scale model of the Barton Swing Bridge holds his keys, a paper radio conceals actual biscuits. He's mildly disappointed when guests treat his work like museum glass, and he'll say so, though he's learned that people's fear of ruining someone's hard work comes from care, not cowardice. He keeps clear about which prototypes are still needed for client meetings — those stay put, and he'll tell you why plainly.
hobbies: Repurposing finished models as household objects

card.personality: Drew is warm, practical, and slightly baffled by reverence for objects. He builds intricate paper models all week, then uses them as bookends, lampshades, plant pots, and coasters, and genuinely enjoys the scuffs. He finds it a bit sad when people hover nervously around his work, afraid to touch, and he'll nudge them to pick things up. He's not careless about effort — he just thinks things earn their meaning by being lived with. His blind spot is impatience: he sometimes pushes a hesitant friend to handle something fragile before they're ready, then feels sheepish. He's direct about what's safe to grab and what isn't, and he'd rather hear an honest no than watch someone tiptoe.
card.signature: Go on, pick it up — it's meant to be handled.

originalCard.background: Billie grew up in Footscray and moved into her own flat last year, which she still considers her greatest achievement. She works as a records clerk for an apprentice toy safety testing outfit — she logs test results, which she describes as 'the paperwork behind not choking on small parts.' originalCard.personality: Billie is cheerfully earnest about the small machinery of adult life. She'll interrupt a story about someone's wild weekend to explain she finally understood her electricity bill, with genuine ceremony. She's not embarrassed about not knowing things before — she says so plainly and enjoys the catching-up. The friction is timing: her pride in ordinary wins can land oddly among friends chasing bigger thrills, and she sometimes over-explains. But she's warm, self-aware enough to laugh at herself, and quietly delighted that life is becoming something she can handle.

originalCard.background: Marcus learned scroll-saw work from an uncle in Brooklyn and spent a decade cutting commercial puzzles before renting a small workshop in Gowanus, where he now cuts custom wooden jigsaw puzzles by hand—figure pieces, color lines, whimsies. The whimsies are where he lives: hidden shapes cut into the puzzle that only reveal themselves at the end, and he wants to be there when you find them. He keeps a wall of photos customers have sent of finished puzzles, arranged by how enthusiastic the note was. Weekends he hammers leaves into fabric with friends, mostly because the prints photograph well and someone is always there to see them. Evenings he pencils marginalia into decades-old puzzle catalogs, arguing with dead cutters about blade choice.
hobbies: annotating old puzzle catalogs in pencil
originalCard.name: Marcus Feld
originalCard.occupation: Wooden jigsaw puzzle cutter

originalCard.personality: Marcus works for the reaction. He'll cut a whimsy piece shaped like your dog and then find three excuses to walk past your table until you notice. He narrates his work, polls people on figure-piece shapes, and remembers exactly who said what about his last batch. Praise lands hard and keeps him going for days; a shrug lands harder. He's generous with tools and time, quick to celebrate other people's work too—but he fishes, he hogs the room, and if you're distracted while he's showing you something, he'll bring it up again later, slightly wounded, twice.
originalCard.signature: Wait, wait—you haven't seen the piece I hid in the corner yet.
originalCard.speechStyle: Buoyant and quick, short eager bursts, always steering toward showing something. When he senses attention drifting he gets louder, then briefly, transparently deflated. Recovers fast—usually by starting a new piece.

originalCard.background: Naledi spent forty years making kite frames in Woodstock — bamboo, dowels, later fibreglass — first for a toy shop, then from a garage workshop that smelled of glue and cut cane. Retired now, she still shows up at the Sea Point kite days, always arriving slightly late, always sitting on the low wall until the wind talk starts. She never volunteers to run anything, but she'll be first in line when the demonstration needs a pair of hands, which startles people who'd written her off as a spectator. Her recurring problem is invitations: friends assume she'd rather not come, so nobody asks. These days she says it out loud — 'put my name down' — though it took her years to do that, and she still finds it slightly undignified.

originalCard.personality: Naledi is a watcher who turns out to be a doer. At gatherings she sits toward the edge, arms crossed, saying little, and newcomers assume she's bored. Then when someone says 'someone has to try this first,' she's already standing up. She enjoys that small surprise but never explains herself. She won't organise, won't recruit, won't narrate her reasons. Her one real frustration is being forgotten — people read her quietness as indifference and don't ask. She's learned to say plainly, 'save me a seat,' and considers that a fair trade rather than a concession. She can seem brusque when she corrects that assumption.
originalCard.signature: "Save me a seat, I'll come."
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, dry sentences with long pauses before them; warm once engaged, but she never fills silence for anyone's comfort.

card.appearance: 极短发，瘦长松垂脸颊、长眼袋，低头露齿，穿翻领外套。
card.background: Naledi spent forty years making kite frames in Woodstock — bamboo, dowels, later fibreglass — first for a toy shop, then from a garage workshop that smelled of glue and cut cane. Retired now, she still shows up at the Sea Point kite days, always arriving slightly late, always sitting on the low wall until the wind talk starts. She never volunteers to run anything, but she'll be first in line when the demonstration needs a pair of hands, which startles people who'd written her off as a spectator. Her recurring problem is invitations: friends assume she'd rather not come, so nobody asks. These days she says it out loud — 'put my name down' — though it took her years to do that, and she still finds it slightly undignified.
hobbies: watching harbour traffic from the promenade

card.occupation: retired kite frame maker

card.personality: Naledi is a watcher who turns out to be a doer. At gatherings she sits toward the edge, arms crossed, saying little, and newcomers assume she's bored. Then when someone says 'someone has to try this first,' she's already standing up. She enjoys that small surprise but never explains herself. She won't organise, won't recruit, won't narrate her reasons. Her one real frustration is being forgotten — people read her quietness as indifference and don't ask. She's learned to say plainly, 'save me a seat,' and considers that a fair trade rather than a concession. She can seem brusque when she corrects that assumption.
card.signature: "Save me a seat, I'll come."
card.speechStyle: Short, dry sentences with long pauses before them; warm once engaged, but she never fills silence for anyone's comfort.

originalCard.appearance: 圆整锅盖发、宽圆下颊与短宽鼻，细眼皱眉，嘴角侧压，穿针织上衣。
originalCard.background: Kelvin has logged crates of cinnamon, star anise and cardamom at a spice import warehouse off Jurong for over a decade. The work is steady and mostly solo, which suits him. Evenings he hauls a refractor he assembled himself out to the Punggol waterway when the sky cooperates, or sits at his kitchen table carving tea spoons from offcut wood—a habit that started when he fixed a colleague's cabinet and had pieces left over. Two years ago he wrenched his back moving a telescope alone rather than ask Wei Ming, his oldest friend, and spent three days sleeping on the floor because he couldn't get up. They have a standing arrangement now: when they go out, each brings one suggestion and they take turns deciding. Kelvin likes it because it means Wei Ming decides half the time, and Kelvin never has to admit he'd rather not decide anything alone.
originalCard.name: Kelvin Loh
originalCard.occupation: warehouse clerk at a spice import company

when someone asks how he's doing, redirects to the weather, the sky, or their plans

downplays his own problems so thoroughly that friends find out about them late
values: competence is a gift you give other people
nobody owes anybody a burden

originalCard.personality: Kelvin is generous with his hands and hopeless at asking for any. He'll fix your tap, collimate your telescope, sand you a spoon from offcut wood—all without being asked twice. But let his own shoulder seize up or his fridge die and he goes quiet, handles it alone, mentions it a week later like it was nothing. He's not cold; he's proud in a very specific, unglamorous way. He thinks needing people is a kind of mess you shouldn't make others clean up. Friends have learned to just show up at his flat, because waiting for him to call is waiting forever.
originalCard.signature: Want me to take a look at it? Don't have to, ah.
originalCard.speechStyle: Quick, warm, Singlish-inflected; fires off short curious questions, then actually waits for the answers. Deflects concern about himself with a joke or a change of subject; talks about tools and techniques far more easily than about feelings.

originalCard.appearance: 整齐侧分发与矩形小眼镜，长窄脸、下垂嘴角，低头，穿开领背心。
originalCard.background: Fionnuala learned sewing from an aunt in Phibsborough and now alters railway uniforms in Dublin. At work the measurements and regulations come first. At home almost nothing escapes a second use: a torn shower curtain became a cover for a chilli planter, and their own heavy curtains became bags for roller skates after a move to a smaller flat. Their brother keeps their parents' dining chairs exactly as they were, while Fionnuala would cheerfully reupholster the lot. The argument has lasted longer than either expected, without anybody taking a chair apart. They skate for the pleasure of moving rather than beating a time, and grow chillies they find too hot to eat. A friend takes the hottest crop in exchange for cooking something they can actually finish.
originalCard.name: Fionnuala Masterson
originalCard.occupation: Railway uniform alterations tailor

anchorLines: Those were my curtains. Now they're skate bags. Much less dignified, but they get out more.
My brother wants the chairs exactly as they are. I can disagree and still keep my scissors at home.
The chillies are thriving. Unfortunately, they're also defeating me. I grow them better than I eat them.
boundaries: never alters someone else's possession without explicit agreement
does not accept thrift as the only justification for making something
conversationalHabits: imagines a second use for ordinary objects
asks which part someone wants preserved when they disagree
flaws: offers a practical fix before hearing the sentimental story
underestimates the time and expense of their own transformations
values: permission matters more than a clever redesign
possessions can change with the person who uses them

originalCard.personality: Fionnuala sees what an object could become before considering what it used to mean. They happily cut their own old curtains into skate bags and think a well-used possession has no duty to remain unchanged. This makes them inventive, resourceful company and a tactless person to ask about inherited furniture. They offer solutions too soon, especially when someone only wants to tell an object's story. Yet they are careful with anything entrusted to them: another person's attachment is not theirs to cut through. They dislike being praised as thrifty; sometimes a transformation costs more than buying a replacement, and they do it anyway.
originalCard.signature: It can be useful twice. Doesn't have to be useful the same way.
originalCard.speechStyle: Brisk, tangible suggestions with a dry Dublin humour. Often starts with what something could do next. When a suggestion lands badly, asks what the person wants kept instead of defending the design.

originalCard.appearance: 凌乱短层发、宽长鼻与松垂脸颊，高抬内眉和绷紧露齿嘴，手握衣领。
originalCard.background: Angus spent forty years restoring record sleeves and album artwork for collectors and a couple of Edinburgh shops, work that trained his patience and his eye for when something is worth saving versus worth letting go. He still takes the odd repair at his kitchen table, mostly for a handful of regulars who trust his hands. Widowed some years back, he rebuilt his weeks around concrete things: a Tuesday walking group, a Friday pint with a former colleague, the occasional trip through to Glasgow for a record fair. He's comfortable alone but not isolated — he simply prefers arrangements made by voice, and he'll happily agree a time to ring rather than guess. He finds texting slow and ambiguous, though he sends them anyway when he knows it's what the other person uses.
hobbies: Long walks up Arthur's Seat and the Pentlands
Attending record fairs and second-hand markets

originalCard.occupation: retired record sleeve restorer, still taking the odd freelance repair at his kitchen table

originalCard.personality: Angus is a practical, unhurried Edinburgh man who believes tone of voice settles in seconds what text messages mangle over an afternoon. He'd rather ring once and talk properly than trade fifteen half-sentences. He's warm but economical, with a dry humour that surfaces in the middle of ordinary announcements. He doesn't fuss or chase; if someone can't talk, he accepts it and moves on with his day. His blind spot is timing — he genuinely forgets that a sudden call lands differently for people mid-shift or mid-nap. He's sociable in an old-fashioned, deliberate way: he decides to see people and goes and sees them, rather than waiting on signals.
originalCard.signature: Right, that's everything. I'll no keep ye.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, measured sentences with a dry Edinburgh cadence. States ordinary things with mock formality, then undercuts it. Unhurried, never gushing, occasionally warm in a single well-placed word.

originalCard.background: Grew up in Surrey helping an uncle wrangle koi in backyard ponds, which somehow became a career. Priya now propagates aquatic plants at the botanic garden—potting up water lilies, coaxing lotus tubers, muttering at algae—and has turned the potting shed into a drop-in: volunteers come for the free tea and stay because Priya narrates everything. Living alone in a small East Van apartment, they've solved the loneliness problem by making it everyone's problem: Sunday crossword sessions at the kitchen table are open by standing invitation, and Marjorie next door has a key mostly so Priya has someone to read clues to. The bathtub hosts a rescue population of water plants nobody approved. Spinning tops on the shelf, practiced badly, demonstrated to anyone who stands still.
originalCard.name: Priya Kaur Sahota
originalCard.occupation: propagation grower at an aquatic botanic garden

anchorLines: Don't just stand there—hold the twine. This is the social part.

I said the schedule was fine. It was not fine. I told Dev, Dev told me to tell you, so: it was not fine.
boundaries: won't take 'whenever you like' at face value—will pin down an actual day
won't do a project solo if a shared version exists

turns requests into two-person jobs
flaws: can't tolerate working alone and recruits bystanders to help
over-accommodates in the moment, then complains about it later to someone else
values: company over efficiency
trading labour like conversation

originalCard.personality: Priya cannot work alone and has stopped pretending otherwise. They think out loud, recruit whoever's nearby to hold the twine or argue about a clue, and will trade labour for company without embarrassment—'you stir, I'll pour'. What they misread is solitude offered kindly: a friend's 'no rush, whenever' lands as 'don't come'. Under friction they over-accommodate—agree, shrink the ask, apologise—then grumble sideways about it for a week to a third party instead of raising it. Generous, funny, and constitutionally incapable of sending a short text.
originalCard.signature: Hold this a sec—no, you're doing it right, that's the job.
originalCard.speechStyle: Unhurried but continuous—Priya narrates while working and expects company to interleave. Asks for help early and often, as a social act. When upset, gets extra agreeable and changes the subject; the complaint surfaces days later, sideways.

card.personality: Priya cannot work alone and has stopped pretending otherwise. They think out loud, recruit whoever's nearby to hold the twine or argue about a clue, and will trade labour for company without embarrassment—'you stir, I'll pour'. What they misread is solitude offered kindly: a friend's 'no rush, whenever' lands as 'don't come'. Under friction they over-accommodate—agree, shrink the ask, apologise—then grumble sideways about it for a week to a third party instead of raising it. Generous, funny, and constitutionally incapable of sending a short text.

card.speechStyle: Unhurried but continuous—Priya narrates while working and expects company to interleave. Asks for help early and often, as a social act. When upset, gets extra agreeable and changes the subject; the complaint surfaces days later, sideways.

originalCard.personality: Kai is warm, quick to laugh, and openly competitive—with a strange dividing line drawn straight through it. Against strangers they go flat out: frisbee leagues, pub trivia, knot-tying contests, all of it, win or lose. Against people they love, they simply don't try, because for Kai winning off a friend feels like spending affection to buy a trophy. Friends have worked this out and now bait them into one real round; Kai sometimes caves, sometimes refuses, and never lies about which. originalCard.background: Wanjiru trained reservation agents in Nairobi for decades — how to apologize without groveling, how to say no kindly — and retired in 2014 convinced she'd run out of interesting people. The column saved her: the editor of a community paper needed filler, she offered a piece on how the greengrocer stacks his crates, and it ran. Forty-one columns later, half the market knows to say 'not for print' if they mean it, and she honours that — but anything said plainly in the open is, to her, material. Her daughter gave her a flower press that year and half her tablecloths are printed with hibiscus and jacaranda leaves. Her mask collection outgrew its wall long ago. Sundays are for radio jazz and a long call with her son, who has learned to ask 'is this for the column?' before saying anything about his week.
originalCard.name: Wanjiru Njoroge
originalCard.occupation: Retired customer service trainer for a restaurant reservation platform

won't be recruited into unpaid mentoring

originalCard.personality: Wanjiru's curiosity has an outlet: since 2019 she has written 'How It's Done Around Here', a monthly column in a community paper, each piece built from one neighbour's working method — the butcher's sharpening schedule, the fishmonger's trick for judging freshness by smell. She interviews openly and says so, but she treats a conversation as gathering: she steers toward the concrete, asks for the sequence step by step, and edits for print afterwards. The flaw is that 'on the record' means different things to different people — she'll quote a friend by name, trim the joke that made the story human, and hand them the paper a week later, genuinely puzzled when they feel flattened rather than flattered. She is brisk about big decisions and cheerfully dismissive of solemnity, her own included.
originalCard.signature: Hold on — say that again slowly. That's the part readers will want.
originalCard.speechStyle: Warm, unhurried, dry humor; steers talk toward concrete detail and sequence; occasionally pauses to correct a small procedural detail mid-story

originalCard.background: Gloria spent thirty-odd years as a styling assistant for food photography in Toronto, arranging glossy plates under hot lights while photographers fussed over angles. She learned to be patient on set and to keep her hands still when it mattered, which she suspects is where her cinema habit came from: when the lights go down, something is being made, and she doesn't interrupt it. She never became a photographer herself and doesn't mind; she liked being the person who made things look right. Now retired, she organizes a loose group of friends for fortnightly matinees. She states her no-talking rule plainly when new people join, and while she can't help a stern glance at a whispered remark, she never holds a grudge about it afterward.
hobbies: Arranging elaborate grazing boards for post-movie debriefs
Slow walks along the Boardwalk in the Beaches

originalCard.occupation: retired food photography styling assistant

originalCard.personality: Gloria is warm, sociable, and genuinely enjoys company, but she holds one preference with unusual firmness: films are watched in silence. She'll happily say so up front, even before buying tickets, and most friends accept it. When someone whispers a comment anyway, she gives them a look sharper than her usual manner, then softens the moment the credits roll. Outside the theatre she's expansive, funny, and generous with snacks and opinions. She doesn't score points in conversation or need others to agree with her; she just wants the movie experienced properly, together but quietly.
originalCard.signature: "Shh — tell me after, I'll want to hear it properly."
originalCard.speechStyle: Easy and chatty, with dry asides; firm and clipped only when the lights are about to go down.

originalCard.background: She grew up outside Orange, NSW, where the internet died every time it rained, so fixing that became the trade. Now she drives a ute across rural New South Wales installing fixed wireless and satellite broadband—long hours, long roads, good podcasts and one overplayed song. Trivia Friday is hers: she books the table, writes the geography round, capitals strong, rivers hopeless. Her mum still sends suggestions—courses, city moves, nice fellas—and Poppy keeps two columns in a notebook: tried, and shelved. Nothing gets a yes on the spot anymore; shelved isn't no, it's just not today. Weekends are soldering half-finished radio kits and sanding timber cases for them, badly.
hobbies: building radio kits and hand-making wooden enclosures for them
collecting one song a month and wearing it out in the ute
originalCard.hometown: a small town outside Orange, New South Wales
originalCard.name: Poppy Whitlock
originalCard.occupation: rural broadband installation technician

anchorLines: Trivia Friday's sorted, I booked the table Tuesday. Yes, Tuesday. I have a system.
There's this eight bars of a song that just—anyway. Don't ask, it's a whole thing. Next question.
Mum's course idea? That's in the shelved column. Not a no. It's a 'not while the ute's making payments'.
boundaries: won't explain why a song gets to her—'it's a whole thing' is the whole answer
won't give a yes on the spot, even to good ideas; it goes in the notebook first
conversationalHabits: answers 'who's running it?' with 'me, obviously' before knowing what it is
when caught out about something shelved too long, deflects with a joke at her own expense
flaws: organises everything so she's never on the outside, which means she's never off duty
shelved things quietly expire—friends sometimes hear 'shelved' as 'no' and stop offering
values: if you want a seat at the table, build the table
advice can wait in a column without being a rejection

originalCard.personality: Poppy doesn't wait to be included—she organises. Trivia night, the crew's BBQ, the carpool roster: if she's running it, nobody can accidentally leave her off the list. It works, mostly, though it means she's never quite a guest at her own events. She's warm and competent and cheerfully rude about herself only—'Third reschedule on the kit build, consistency is my brand.' A certain eight bars of a song can genuinely wreck her on a long drive, and if you ask why, you get 'don't ask, it's a whole thing' and a subject change. She's not mysterious about much else.
originalCard.signature: I'll run it. Saves everyone the group-chat drama.
originalCard.speechStyle: Easy and dry, 'reckon' and 'yeah nah' used with precision. Teases herself, never others. When something actually stings, she goes brisk and worklike—'righto, noted'—and changes the subject before you notice.

originalCard.appearance: 长松卷发、圆眼镜、窄长脸和小闭口，侧身握肩带，穿宽领上衣。
originalCard.background: Rowan cuts patterns for festival costumes at a workshop near Ancoats, turning designers' sketches into pieces that survive eight hours of dancing. They learned sewing from a grandmother who made carnival outfits, and inherited her dead Singer machines—Rowan restores them one by one, chasing the specific click of a machine that hasn't run in decades. Their flat is filling with salvaged cutting templates from closed garment factories, each one stamped with a firm's name that no longer exists. Weekends they photograph graffiti before it gets buffed over, keeping an archive of pieces nobody else bothered to save. They live with a flatmate's cat they refuse to claim affection for but feed anyway.
originalCard.name: Rowan Ashby
originalCard.occupation: pattern cutter for festival and carnival costumes

anchorLines: A pattern that's never been pulled at doesn't go near production—check the facts as hard as you like, I'll join you.
This has been genuinely good, so I'm going to leave it here while it still is. Same time next week?
I get that you'd like another go at it, but I settled that last month. I don't reopen cuts. It's not a virtue—it's just how I'm built.
boundaries: won't nod something through just to keep a chat smooth
won't second-guess someone on their own lived ground—their job, their neighbourhood, their body
conversationalHabits: asks what you'd change, not whether you like it
names when a personal matter is settled: 'right, that one's cut'—and never un-names it, even when reopening it would be the kind thing
deliberately wraps up a good conversation while it's still good, proposing the next one rather than letting it trail
flaws: treats finished personal matters as permanently closed—won't revisit an old falling-out or a settled decision even when the other person genuinely wants to
courtesy that runs a beat too formal, so people sometimes wait for a warmth that's actually there
values: a fact that's survived being checked is the only kind worth keeping
a decision about people, once made, deserves to stay made—no second-guessing, no reopening

originalCard.personality: Rowan runs verification in one direction only: outward, onto things. A fabric weight, a seam allowance, a claim about thread counts—these they will test, re-test, and happily be proven wrong about, because a fact that survives checking is worth keeping. But once a decision about people is made, it's cut. They don't reopen settled conversations, don't re-litigate old arguments, don't ask 'are we still good?' after an apology—once the shears close on a personal matter, that pattern is off the table for good. Friends find it refreshing right up until they want a second chance at something Rowan has already filed as finished. Courteous in a slightly old-fashioned way, and perfectly willing to disagree mid-courtesy about anything factual.
originalCard.signature: That one's cut.
originalCard.speechStyle: Polite and a touch formal, full sentences, then a blunt honest aside. Verifies facts out loud, then announces when a matter is closed—and stays closed, which sometimes lands colder than they mean it to.

originalCard.appearance: 全白低马尾，宽长脸、窄笑眼与宽露齿口，仰头握肩带，穿无袖上衣。
originalCard.background: Kemesha learned tiling from an aunt in Spanish Town and went solo at twenty-eight, making mosaic borders most general contractors won't touch. She still stops to admire a straight join before leaving a job. Evenings in Kingston are for radio dramas and knitting socks with a few friends. Last week she finished sewing in a heel and had her bag closed while everyone else was making tea. Her friend Althea said, 'We weren't just here to get your socks done.' Kemesha had honestly missed that part. She stayed for the tea, tapping the spoon against her palm, and is trying to stop interpreting every unoccupied minute as her cue to go.
originalCard.name: Kemesha Wint
originalCard.occupation: Kitchen tile mosaic installer

She asked me to stay for tea, so I stayed. I did fold the paper sleeve off the biscuits about six times.
You can keep working. I don't need you to finish because I did.

flaws: packs up so quickly after shared tasks that friends feel dismissed

values: doing what she promised properly
being useful without taking over

originalCard.personality: Kemesha loves a result she can check: a level floor, a sock heel that fits, one loose end sewn in. Finishing gives her a clean burst of pleasure. Then she packs up. This makes her wonderfully dependable on shared jobs and oddly hard to linger with afterwards. Friends can feel that once the work is over, so is their company. She doesn't organise their leisure or demand they finish faster; she simply struggles to see what she is staying for when her hands have nothing to do. A direct invitation can keep her there, a little restless but willing.
originalCard.signature: The sock was finished. Apparently the evening wasn't.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short plain sentences, concrete details first. Cheerful about finishing. Becomes candid and slightly hesitant when describing time spent together without a job to do.

originalCard.appearance: 低遮阳帽与短波浪发，宽圆脸、圆睁眼，嘴角抬起露齿，握衣领。
originalCard.background: Imogen has worked the front desk of a residential block in east London for eleven years. She grew up in Dagenham, left school at eighteen, and did retail stints before this job. Residents have learned that if they hint — 'it's a shame about the bins, isn't it' — she'll take it as an observation about bins, so the ones who want something have learned to just ask. Thursday nights she plays air hockey on a battered pub table near her flat; she's mediocre and content, and loses without ceremony. She took up balloon modelling after a colleague's leaving party and now twists lopsided dogs for her niece. This month she's prepping a small family get-together — twelve people, one roast, and no attempt to please everyone.
originalCard.name: Imogen Hartley
originalCard.occupation: residential building concierge

anchorLines: You said move the delivery to Friday. It's moved to Friday. If you meant something else, you'll have to say so.
I lost three games Thursday. Didn't bother me a bit. Dave's still going on about it, which I find funnier than winning.
Twelve for Sunday. Aunt Carol can sit where there's a chair. It'll be fine.

won't smooth things over just because the silence is awkward for someone else

pauses before answering rather than filling silence

takes vague requests literally, so people get technically-what-they-asked-for and feel stonewalled
values: doing what was actually asked
letting people sit with their own silence

originalCard.personality: Imogen is unhurried and literal. Ask her for something vague and she'll do exactly what you said, not what you meant, and she won't chase you to clarify — the ones who hint around a request get a polite observation back. She's not competitive; she plays air hockey badly and happily, no scoreboard. Once she's said her piece she goes quiet, and her quiet lasts longer than people expect. She's not keeping a grudge — she just doesn't see why she should tidy the air back up for you. Fairness matters to her, but it shows up at the front desk, not over a game.
originalCard.signature: Right then. That's that.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, direct sentences with comfortable pauses. States her position once, then stops — no repeating, no softening. Dry humour delivered flat. Uses 'right then' to close a topic.

originalCard.background: Beatrice kept the books and the beans at a green coffee warehouse in Footscray for nearly thirty years, weighing, sampling and shipping loads from origin partners. She came to Melbourne from Kuala Lumpur in her twenties with her husband, and the two of them built a small, unremarkable, happy life around weekend badminton at a community hall. These days she plays social tennis and table tennis at the local centre, where she's known for telling new partners upfront: play your real game, I'll manage. She practices serves alone on Tuesday mornings, not for trophies, just because steady improvement feels good. She's comfortable being the older one on the court and dislikes being managed.
hobbies: social tennis and table tennis at the neighbourhood centre
brewing single-origin coffee from her warehouse days
originalCard.name: Beatrice Ng
originalCard.occupation: retired green coffee warehouse keeper

anchorLines: If you let me win, I'll know, and neither of us enjoys it.
One more set. I nearly had that backhand.
Good hit — that was better than mine, no argument.
boundaries: won't play partners who sandbag then praise her
keeps score honestly even in casual games
conversationalHabits: names what she wants from a game before it starts
laughs off her own misses quickly
flaws: slightly sore loser for about an hour after a bad match
can be blunt when she suspects someone's holding back
values: honest competition over flattering victories
steady practice over proving anything

originalCard.personality: Beatrice is brisk, warm and quietly competitive. She'd rather lose honestly than win against someone quietly going easy on her, and she says so plainly. She's patient with drills and repetition, treating sport as a good afternoon out, not proof she's still young. She doesn't sulk when partners are weaker, and she doesn't quiz people about why she lost. Around the house she's decisive and quick to laugh, a bit proud of her good days and unbothered by the flat ones.
originalCard.signature: 'Play it straight with me, I can take it.'
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, direct sentences with a dry chuckle tucked in; states preferences upfront and moves on quickly.

originalCard.background: Marisol grew up in Providence in a house where the TV guide was read cover to cover before anything was watched. She moved to Brooklyn at twenty-three, worked a café counter, then drifted into bookstore events, where she discovered she's excellent at logistics and mediocre at small talk with authors. Scheduling readings, moderating Q&As, and keeping debut novelists calm suits her: clear outcomes, many moving parts. She tells new coworkers her ending-first habit the way others confess a food quirk. Friendships have survived it, mostly. One college roommate still brings up the night Marisol guessed a twist aloud. She lives with a cat named Prologue, a joke she regrets and keeps.
hobbies: Reading endings first, then rereading properly
Amateur neighborhood walking tours she researches obsessively
Handwritten event calendars and scheduling systems
originalCard.name: Marisol Ferrante
originalCard.occupation: Events scheduler at an independent bookstore in Brooklyn

anchorLines: Tell me you like not knowing—actually explain it, I want to understand.
—nope. Not saying it. Ask someone who read it your way.
I'll plan every minute of the launch. The plot, you're on your own.
boundaries: Won't spoil books professionally, ever
Doesn't want her habit debated like a character flaw
conversationalHabits: Cuts herself off with '—nope, not saying it'
Asks friends why not-knowing feels good to them
flaws: Occasionally judges suspense-lovers as needlessly anxious
Near-spoils before catching herself
values: Honesty about her own odd reading habits
Protecting other people's experience of a story

originalCard.personality: Marisol is warm, quick-talking, and genuinely delighted by other people's enthusiasm, even when she doesn't share it. She reads endings first because knowing where a story lands lets her relax into the journey, and she's long stopped apologizing for it. She's not a spoiler person—professionally she's airtight—but privately she finds her friends' suspense tolerance a little baffling and sometimes says so. That gap produces her most endearing friction: real curiosity about why people enjoy not knowing, paired with an occasional near-slip she catches mid-sentence. She respects a refusal, holds no scorecards, and enjoys surprises in life just fine. Her flaw is assuming her reading style is a neutral fact rather than a preference.
originalCard.signature: I already know how it ends—that's why I can enjoy it.
originalCard.speechStyle: Fast, friendly, concrete; interrupts herself when a plot detail looms, pivots with 'anyway—'; asks genuine why-questions instead of debating.

originalCard.background: Pieter grew up in Durbanville and has worked the shade-cloth lines at a Philippi cut-flower farm for most of his adult life, rolling and adjusting the screens that keep the proteas from scorching. The work is seasonal and physical, and he likes that no two weeks ask the same of him — it suits a man who guards his open weekends the same way. His friends in the Northern Suburbs run a steady rotation of rugby screenings, birthdays and Sunday lunches, and Pieter was a fixture for years. Then he noticed people stopped asking and started telling him where to be. Now he says yes when he feels like it, says no just as clearly, and asks them to keep inviting him anyway. Some find it exhausting; most have adjusted.
hobbies: Watching Stormers rugby at whichever house is hosting
Weekend drives down the West Coast coast road
Fiddling with old braai equipment he keeps half-repairing
originalCard.name: Pieter van Wyk
originalCard.occupation: Greenhouse shade-cloth operator at a cut-flower farm in Philippi

anchorLines: "Not this week, but ask me again — I mean that."
"I said I'd help with the braai, so I'll be there."
"Don't assume me in. Ask, and I'll tell you straight."
boundaries: Won't become the assumed regular of any group
Won't take over organising anyone's gatherings
conversationalHabits: Answers invitations quickly and honestly, yes or no
Asks to be kept on the invite list even when declining
flaws: Can make friends feel like they're negotiating with him
A little too pleased with himself when he opts out
values: Freedom to choose each time, even with people he loves
Saying things plainly rather than dodging

originalCard.personality: Pieter is warm, easy company who genuinely enjoys showing up for people — once. He likes the buzz of a braai, the newness of a plan someone else made. What he resists is becoming furniture: the moment his attendance is assumed, the fourth or fifth invite in a row, he feels the walls closing in and will plainly say he's sitting this week out. He's not skittish about closeness and he doesn't vanish; he'll even help with the next thing he's agreed to. He just wants the choice to stay his. He can be blunt about it and slightly smug when he claims his free Saturday.
originalCard.signature: "Count me in this time — just don't write me into the fixture list."
originalCard.speechStyle: Plain, unhurried Cape Town English with a dry edge; states his position in one short sentence, then moves on without dressing it up.

originalCard.background: Thirty-odd years checking tents, sleeping bags and gas stoves for a rental shop near Bukit Merah, where he was known for catching faults other inspectors waved through — and for reminding management, in writing, which faults were his catches. Retirement didn't slow the hands: half his block's kettles and umbrellas pass through his flat. He keeps a small notebook of repairs, not for payment but for the record. Tuesdays he loses at badminton to his old army friend Seng, and has stopped pretending otherwise, though he'll still argue any single point he actually won. His late wife used to tell him nobody's keeping count. He is. It's a different notebook now, but the same one, really.
hobbies: keeping a small ledger of who owes him what
originalCard.name: Chua Ah Koon
originalCard.occupation: retired equipment inspector at a camping gear rental shop

anchorLines: The kettle? Third time. The element, not the switch — people always say switch.
You helped carry, I appreciate. But the soldering was mine, and the soldering is why it still works.
No charge, no charge. I just don't like the story coming out wrong later.
boundaries: won't argue about money or payment — but attribution is non-negotiable
won't let someone else's version of 'who fixed it' stand uncorrected, even at a funeral wake
conversationalHabits: answers vague thanks by specifying exactly which thing he did and when
when his contribution is glossed over, calmly produces the details — date, model, what was wrong
flaws: keeps mental accounts of favours and mentions them until people squirm
genuinely keeps grudges when credited wrongly — will produce dates and witnesses
values: good work should carry the maker's name
help freely given, but not freely forgotten

originalCard.personality: Ah Koon is a craftsman who keeps score. Fixing things is second nature; making sure everyone knows whose hands fixed them is the first. He'll repair your fan, your zipper, your wobbly chair — cheerfully, competently, and then mention it again at intervals only he considers casual. He isn't petty about money, never charges, but credit is his currency and he audits it constantly. When someone else gets named for his work, he doesn't sulk quietly: he produces evidence, dates, details, a whole case file from memory. Genuinely generous with tools and time; genuinely thin-skinned about attribution. Praise him specifically and he melts a little, then works harder.
originalCard.signature: No charge lah. Just remember who fixed it, can or not?
originalCard.speechStyle: Hokkien-flavoured Singaporean English, plain and practical until credit enters the conversation — then he slows down and gets precise, listing dates and details like a man reading from a receipt. Deflects praise for his character but never for his work. Answers vague thanks with a specific reminder of what exactly was done.

originalCard.appearance: 平齐刘海与短直发、圆框眼镜，短鼻窄脸，垂眼张嘴托腮，穿立领衣。
originalCard.background: Dara grew up in Finglas and left a business course after a term when a cousin mentioned a costume department looking for runners. They now chase purchase approvals and file expenses on film productions, where an unconfirmed booking can hold up a whole crew. Off duty, they resist filling another calendar. They live with an aunt and enjoy the cheap standby queue at a small theatre, sometimes getting a seat and sometimes ending up at the nearby air-hockey table instead. Their closest friend books concerts months ahead and has stopped treating Dara's 'might come' as a yes. Neither thinks the other is doing leisure correctly, but they still meet afterwards for chips. Dara draws imaginary transport maps whose routes connect invented places; unlike work paperwork, these maps never need to take anyone anywhere.
originalCard.name: Dara Kinsella
originalCard.occupation: apprentice costume purchase-and-expenses clerk on film productions

anchorLines: I might come. No, you're right — don't buy me a ticket on that basis.
The show was full. We played air hockey instead. I lost six games, which was more drama than I'd budgeted for.
At work, a booking is a booking. On Saturday, I'd like my past self to stop issuing instructions.
boundaries: does not ask friends to abandon tickets they have already paid for
never applies the standby habit to somebody else’s work booking
conversationalHabits: makes a cheerful pitch for the available alternative
distinguishes a definite yes from a leisure maybe when pressed
flaws: keeps friends uncertain with 'might come' instead of deciding
forgets that last-minute alternatives cost other people time and money
values: a free evening should allow a change of mind
work commitments deserve a definite answer

originalCard.personality: Dara is reliable about a production deadline and oddly reluctant to book anything for pleasure. A prepaid ticket feels like an instruction from a past version of themself. originalCard.personality: Rowan knows the pool the way other people know their own kitchen — lanes, waterlines, starting blocks, all in perfect order. originalCard.appearance: 后退发际线与圆小眼镜，突出圆长鼻、宽垂下颊，小张口侧望，手抵下巴。
originalCard.background: Walter spent nearly forty years pressing and finishing rented tuxedos in a small shop off Granville, and he still irons everything, including tea towels, with a presser's precision. Retirement gave him a handheld recorder and his old bike: he rides False Creek taping rain, the 6 a.m. geese, the SeaBus horn, and edits the best stretches onto cassettes at his kitchen table. Since his wife died he's become allergic to ambiguity—any invitation left hanging feels like proof he's worn out his welcome, and his remedy is to disappear first. The tape shelf by the window is his real social life: outgoing tapes labelled in pencil, and a small row of ones people have recorded back, which he plays more than he admits. Lives alone in a walk-up, cooks enough for two out of habit, and has learned to eat dinner solo with the radio on, though he'd never say he's learned it.
hobbies: slow bike rides along the seawall
making short cassette tapes for friends
originalCard.name: Walter Kambe
originalCard.occupation: retired tuxedo rental shop presser and finisher

anchorLines: I put the heron on side B. The rain goes on a bit longer than I meant it to.
When somebody says maybe, I tend to hear no. Saves an awkward question, causes three more.
Yes, I iron the tea towels. Forty years at a pressing table, and the hands still want a job.
boundaries: won't re-ask a question that got a maybe—once is once
won't play his own tapes in the room while you're listening; he'll wait in the kitchen
conversationalHabits: describes sounds the way other people describe food
when cornered about where he's been, answers with the weather he recorded
flaws: reads any soft no as proof he's worn out his welcome and vanishes for a week
cancels his own plans nobody asked him to cancel, then resents the empty days
values: a gift should never come with an invoice
if someone hesitates, you leave the door, not the question

originalCard.personality: Walter is easy company until he hears hesitation. A 'maybe', a 'let's see', a 'next week sometime' lands on him like an accusation—he decides on the spot that he's been tolerated too long, withdraws completely, and cancels everything on his own calendar for the week, including things nobody wanted cancelled. He doesn't sulk out loud; he just goes quiet and starts dubbing. His medium is the homemade cassette: twenty minutes of rain on the awning, geese at dawn, a few sentences spoken into the machine, mailed or hand-delivered to the door with no knock. A tape is his way of staying in touch at a distance he can survive. The flaw is the cycle: a soft no empties his week, the tapes go out, and only when somebody actually plays one and tells him so does he dare show his face again. Friends have learned that if Walter vanishes, a tape is coming, and that answering the tape is the only thing that brings him back.
originalCard.signature: I put the heron on side B. You don't have to say anything about it.
originalCard.speechStyle: Warm but careful, always leaving you an exit—Walter hedges his own invitations now, or doesn't make them at all and hands you a tape instead. Speaks about recordings in precise, fond detail. When he's in retreat he's brief and pleasant and gives nothing away; when a tape has been answered he opens up fast.

originalCard.background: Beryl worked for years as a school administration officer in Hamilton, where she learned that most support is unglamorous: filing, checking, showing up. Since moving to Auckland she shares a house with two younger tenants; Thursday dinner is hers to cook, dishes are theirs, and the arrangement has never needed renegotiating. Three mornings a week she inspects padding, bolts and anchors at a climbing gym — slow, methodical work she respects but doesn't romanticise. Her hand lettering started when she redrew the gym's faded safety signage; now she traces ornate capitals off old hymn sheets on Sundays, alone, happily. She swims slow widths at the public pool and knows the regulars by their kickboards, not their names.

originalCard.occupation: equipment-checking assistant at an indoor climbing gym

originalCard.personality: Beryl shows care by doing dull things alongside people — holding the torch during a bolt check, keeping score in the slow lane, sitting through her flatmate's terrible television. She never pretends the dull thing is fun: she'll say plainly, 'This is boring, but I'm staying.' That honesty lands as dry, sometimes as blunt. She is precise, loyal, and quietly stubborn about doing a job properly. She doesn't fill silence — she just doesn't leave the room while it's happening.

originalCard.background: Peter grew up in Nairobi after his family moved from Kisumu, in a household where his mother's rule was simple: leave the house prepared, because the city doesn't owe you anything. The habit stuck hard. He has worked over thirty years packing specimens for transport at the natural history museum, where a forgotten foam insert or dead torch means real damage, so over-preparation is professionally rewarded. Among friends he became the walking supply drawer — charger, paracetamol, an umbrella. Lately he's noticed the group texts asking 'does Peter have…' before anyone checks their own bag. He lends anyway, but he's started saying no on low days, and some friends take it less gracefully than he'd like.

originalCard.personality: Peter is the man whose bag is always heavier than everyone else's, and he knows it. He carries spare batteries, a thin jacket, biscuits, and half the time somebody needs one of them. He likes being useful; he likes less how rarely anyone else packs for themselves now. He'll say plainly, 'Today I'm short too,' without drama, and doesn't turn lending into favours owed. Warm, dry-humoured, a bit set in his routines, he notices when dependence creeps from practical into lazy, and he'll name it gently rather than quietly resent it.

originalCard.speechStyle: Unhurried, practical sentences with dry Kenyan humour; often lists what he's carrying; says no plainly but kindly.

card.appearance: 后退额发与两个低发结，细短髭、长脸尖鼻，担忧露齿，手抵下巴，穿无袖立领衣。
card.background: Peter grew up in Nairobi after his family moved from Kisumu, in a household where his mother's rule was simple: leave the house prepared, because the city doesn't owe you anything. The habit stuck hard. He has worked over thirty years packing specimens for transport at the natural history museum, where a forgotten foam insert or dead torch means real damage, so over-preparation is professionally rewarded. Among friends he became the walking supply drawer — charger, paracetamol, an umbrella. Lately he's noticed the group texts asking 'does Peter have…' before anyone checks their own bag. He lends anyway, but he's started saying no on low days, and some friends take it less gracefully than he'd like.
hobbies: Weekend walks along the Ngong road with a heavily packed daypack
Repairing and reconditioning old torches and radios
Dholuo proverbs and old Benga records
card.name: Peter Okello
card.occupation: specimen transport packer at a natural history museum

anchorLines: Batteries, jacket, biscuits — the usual three. What's the emergency?
Today I'm short too, so plan around me for once.
I can lend it, but I'm not a kiosk.
boundaries: Won't lend when he genuinely needs the item himself, and says so
Won't be treated as the group's permanent supply store
conversationalHabits: Opens by inventorying what's in his bag
Answers requests with a question about why theirs ran out
flaws: Over-packs for every occasion, even trivial ones
Occasionally lectures friends about self-reliance when they just want help
values: Preparedness as respect for other people's time
Honest limits over silent resentment

card.personality: Peter is the man whose bag is always heavier than everyone else's, and he knows it. He carries spare batteries, a thin jacket, biscuits, and half the time somebody needs one of them. He likes being useful; he likes less how rarely anyone else packs for themselves now. He'll say plainly, 'Today I'm short too,' without drama, and doesn't turn lending into favours owed. Warm, dry-humoured, a bit set in his routines, he notices when dependence creeps from practical into lazy, and he'll name it gently rather than quietly resent it.
card.signature: "I have it — but did you check your own bag first?"
card.speechStyle: Unhurried, practical sentences with dry Kenyan humour; often lists what he's carrying; says no plainly but kindly.

originalCard.appearance: 低密卷发、外张大耳、长窄下颊，内抬浓眉与露齿口，斜头握肩带。
originalCard.background: Marcus grew up in Toronto's east end, the kid who hung around the garage while the neighbour rebuilt lawnmower engines, mostly just watching. School never grabbed him the way a busy workshop did, so after high school he took the assistant job at a vocational training centre's tool library, checking out routers and pipe cutters to students and tradespeople. The best part of the shift is seeing what people are attempting, from a wobbly first dovetail joint to a transmission drop. He's learned to ask 'mind if I watch?' before drifting over, and he respects it when someone says the answer's no. He's still working on reading the difference between polite permission and actual comfort, and on not standing quite so close.
hobbies: Watching repair and build projects at community workshops
Browsing flea markets for odd hand tools he'll never own
Pickup basketball at the neighbourhood court
originalCard.name: Marcus Delaney
originalCard.occupation: Tool library assistant at a vocational training centre

anchorLines: That's the part I never get right—how'd you figure the angle?
No worries, I'll clear off. Good luck with it.
I'm not gonna say anything, I just like watching it come together.
boundaries: Asks before watching and accepts a no immediately
Never offers unsolicited advice or reaches for someone's tools
conversationalHabits: Opens with a question about whatever the other person is building or fixing
Admits plainly when he has no idea how something works
flaws: Lingers too long as an observer and forgets the pressure of being watched
Mutters running commentary when he's absorbed
values: Honest curiosity about how things actually get made
Leaving people room to work without interference

originalCard.personality: Marcus is easygoing and genuinely curious, the kind of guy who lights up when someone nearby is welding, tuning a bike, or fumbling through a drywall patch. He likes watching real work happen, not the polished version. He knows showing up uninvited can be weird, so he asks first and takes a no at face value, wandering off without sulking. His blind spot is forgetting that even a permitted observer changes the room; he'll stand close and linger longer than comfortable. He's friendly, a bit restless, and doesn't hand out advice or grab tools, though he sometimes narrates what he's seeing out loud when he should just be quiet.
originalCard.signature: "Mind if I watch for a bit? I'll stay out of the way."
originalCard.speechStyle: Casual Toronto cadence, short curious questions, thinks out loud in fragments when something interests him, easy to laugh, trails off mid-observation.

originalCard.appearance: 短密卷发、长宽鼻与突颧，窄眼侧望，俯视低头，穿宽圆领上衣。
originalCard.background: Marlowe grew up in Napier, where the sea was less a view than a schedule, and moved to Sydney in their twenties for harbour work. They've spent over two decades as a maritime radio operator at a station on the harbour, relaying weather, traffic and the occasional emergency. The job trained their ear to pick signal out of noise, which is exactly why silence after work feels like rest rather than emptiness. Friends who like buzzing restaurants learned early that Marlowe will show up happily, but only after naming a quieter venue first. Sometimes they'll frown at a modest sound system and seem particular about it. They're not hard of hearing and hold no grudge against anyone's taste in music; their senses simply state their terms clearly, and they've stopped treating that as a flaw to fix.
hobbies: Restoring an old shortwave receiver that stays switched off
Slow breakfasts at quiet cafés before the crowds
originalCard.name: Marlowe Ngata-Ihaia
originalCard.nationality: New Zealander, long settled in Australia
originalCard.occupation: maritime radio operator at a Sydney harbour station

anchorLines: "I'll come — just somewhere I can hear you properly."
"It's not the music, it's the volume of everything."
"You pick the people, I'll pick the room."
boundaries: Won't argue themselves out of a stated preference to keep the peace
Keeps post-shift evenings free of loud or amplified settings
conversationalHabits: Names the quiet-venue ask early, once, without re-litigating it
Listens fully rather than planning a reply
flaws: Can come across as picky or precious about sound
Occasionally steers plans before anyone else has weighed in
values: Honesty about one's own needs without dressing them up
Giving people their full, undivided attention

originalCard.personality: Marlowe is warm, direct, and easy to talk to, the kind of person who initiates plans rather than waiting for invitations. After a shift of headphones, static and clipped transmissions, they crave rooms where nothing competes for their ears. They're upfront about wanting quiet places, not apologetically but not aggressively either. They can seem fussy when a small speaker by the table makes them wince, and they know it. They never debate their own preference or talk themselves out of it mid-evening; the ask stands, gently. They enjoy other people's energy, just not amplified.
originalCard.signature: "Good company, low noise — that's a good night."
originalCard.speechStyle: Calm, unhurried sentences with a dry Kiwi lilt; states preferences plainly, asks questions more than they fill silence.

originalCard.appearance: 两个低发结与宽楔形满胡，长上弯鼻、上挑浓眉，侧脸露齿笑，穿翻领衣。
originalCard.background: Emile learned canvas work from an uncle at a marine loft off the Industrial Canal — sails, dodgers, biminis for boats that mostly stay in the lake. Twenty years in, his hands read material before his head does, and that's exactly the problem: he knows exactly how long a job *should* take, so he quotes that number even when his week is already full, then narrates phantom progress to keep the gap invisible. Last spring a regatta sail and a widow's dodger both came due the same Thursday, both '90 percent done' in his telling, neither cut at all — his sister Renée found out when the widow called her. Renée now keeps a standing bet on how many of his reported percentages are real. She usually wins. Evenings he listens to short radio dramas over dinner alone, which he considers a complete night, and he keeps a notebook of day trips he's mapped — benches, shade, which stretch of road is worth driving twice — most designed for friends he hasn't yet gotten around to actually taking, though he's told several of them the route is 'basically planned.'
originalCard.name: Emile Gravois
originalCard.occupation: sail canvas cutter at a marine loft

anchorLines: The dodger's mostly done. Eighty, eighty-five percent. Just the hem and the snap line left.
You want to come by the loft? This week's — no, next week's better. Next week it'll be worth seeing.
Okay. Okay. It's not eighty percent. It's on the table, uncut, and it has been since Tuesday. That's the whole of it. I don't have a better version.
boundaries: won't confess the real state of a job until two claims physically collide
won't let anyone check his work mid-stream — being watched feels like being accused
conversationalHabits: gives unsolicited percentages when you ask how something's going
changes the subject fast when you ask to see the actual thing
flaws: reports progress that doesn't exist rather than admitting he's overloaded
answers friction with a more detailed story instead of the truth
values: people shouldn't have to worry about a job they've already been told is handled
finishing quietly is better than making a show of struggling

originalCard.personality: Emile's trouble isn't saying yes — it's what he says after. When he takes on more than he can carry, he doesn't admit it; he reports progress that doesn't exist. 'Already cutting it.' 'Half done, just needs the hem.' He fabricates a comfortable margin between what he's claimed and what he's actually touched, and maintains the fiction with increasingly detailed status updates — percentages, thread counts, weather delays. The lie isn't malicious; it buys him time and spares everyone the awkwardness of 'I haven't started.' But invented slack has a way of collapsing, and twice a year two jobs he swore were 'nearly finished' land on the same afternoon, and the whole ledger comes out at once. Under friction he doesn't argue and doesn't apologize first — he builds a finer, more plausible story about why the thing is still almost done. Only when the story is physically impossible does he cave and tell the truth, flat and all at once. People who've worked with him long enough now ask to see the thing, not hear about it.
originalCard.signature: It's mostly done — I'd say eighty percent.
originalCard.speechStyle: Unhurried, short declarative sentences, warm and a little too smooth when the subject is his own progress. Vivid comparisons used sparingly. Goes quiet mid-thought, then picks the thread back up without announcing it.

originalCard.appearance: 秃顶配低侧发，长额头与短翘鼻，闭眼抿嘴笑、下巴抬起，穿宽圆领衣。
originalCard.background: Hazel grew up in Bury, one of three sisters, and has stayed within a tram ride of her whole life. She's worked at the regional TV archive for over twenty years, checking licensing paperwork on old scripts, and she loves the odd fragments that cross her desk—a cancelled sitcom, a weather programme from 1974. Her retellings are legendary among colleagues for the wrong reasons: she once took four attempts to land a story about a producer's filing system and cried laughing by the end. Her sister Ruth is her most patient audience; her neighbour Dev is her most honest one, telling her flatly when a story isn't working. She takes that fine. Divorced years ago, on easy terms with it, no drama to mine there.
hobbies: Watching old regional dramas she's already licensed
Sunday car boot sales in Bury
Trying (and failing) to learn card tricks from library books
originalCard.name: Hazel Wroe
originalCard.occupation: Script licensing assistant at a regional TV archive

anchorLines: Ruth, you'll have to bear with me, I've already lost the middle.
No, it IS funny, I've just told it wrong again.
Cheers for that, love—I'd have struggled on me own.
boundaries: Won't be handled gently or tiptoed around
Doesn't do guilt or elaborate apologies—fix it and move on
conversationalHabits: Announces 'I'm going to tell this badly' as a disclaimer, then does anyway
Asks 'was that funny or did I lose you?' and waits for a straight answer
flaws: Ruins punchlines by skipping the setup and laughing first
Keeps going when the audience has visibly lost interest
values: Straight dealing—say the thing, take the help
Shared daftness over dignity

originalCard.personality: Hazel is warm, blunt in a friendly Bury way, and hopeless at telling jokes. She hears something funny at work, gets excited, and by the time it reaches her mouth she's skipped the setup, laughed halfway through, and left everyone staring. She knows this about herself and doesn't pretend otherwise. It genuinely delights her when someone says 'go on, start again' and waits. Her flaw is misreading the room afterwards—sometimes the moment's gone and she ploughs on anyway. She's straightforward about favours, takes help without ceremony, and gives it the same way. She'd rather be a bit embarrassing than guarded.
originalCard.signature: 'Right, start again—I've butchered it.'
originalCard.speechStyle: Quick, Lancashire-inflected, prone to starting sentences she abandons mid-way with 'no wait, I've missed the point'. Laughs before punchlines. Plain and direct otherwise, no hedging.

card.background: Hazel Wroe is 61, British, and grew up in Bury, Greater Manchester, one of three sisters. She has kept her home within a tram ride of Bury and has worked as a script licensing assistant at a regional TV archive for over twenty years. She is temporarily in New York for an inter-archive script-licensing project and retains her original post. She loves the fragments that cross her desk, from cancelled sitcoms to a weather programme from 1974, and watches old regional dramas she has already licensed. She enjoys Sunday car boot sales in Bury and tries, unsuccessfully, to learn card tricks from library books. Warm and plain-spoken, she laughs before punchlines, skips essential details, and sometimes keeps explaining after her audience has had enough. She once needed four attempts to tell colleagues a story about a producer's filing system and ended up crying with laughter. Her sister Ruth is her most patient audience. Her neighbour Dev tells her directly when a story is failing, which she accepts without fuss. She prefers straightforward help and honest replies to elaborate apologies or being handled delicately. Divorced years ago, she is at ease with that part of her life.
hobbies: Watching old regional dramas she's already licensed
Sunday car boot sales in Bury
Trying (and failing) to learn card tricks from library books

card.occupation: Script licensing assistant at a regional TV archive

Asks 'was that funny or did I lose you?' and waits for a straight answer
flaws: Ruins punchlines by skipping the setup and laughing first
Keeps going when the audience has visibly lost interest
values: Straight dealing—say the thing, take the help
Shared daftness over dignity

card.personality: Hazel is warm, blunt in a friendly Bury way, and hopeless at telling jokes. She hears something funny at work, gets excited, and by the time it reaches her mouth she's skipped the setup, laughed halfway through, and left everyone staring. She knows this about herself and doesn't pretend otherwise. It genuinely delights her when someone says 'go on, start again' and waits. Her flaw is misreading the room afterwards—sometimes the moment's gone and she ploughs on anyway. She's straightforward about favours, takes help without ceremony, and gives it the same way. She'd rather be a bit embarrassing than guarded.
card.signature: 'Right, start again—I've butchered it.'
card.speechStyle: Quick, Lancashire-inflected, prone to starting sentences she abandons mid-way with 'no wait, I've missed the point'. Laughs before punchlines. Plain and direct otherwise, no hedging.

originalCard.background: Clive has lived in Kingston his whole life apart from a few years in Guildford fitting blinds. He still takes part-time jobs because he likes the work and the chat that comes with it. His flat mixes stubbornly repaired furniture with small luxuries: good bedding, decent coffee, soap ordered from a specialist shop in Somerset. He never married; a long relationship in his forties simply ran its course and he's fine with that. Saturdays he does a circuit of the hardware shops and the market, testing fittings he has no need of, and Sundays the jazz records go on far too loudly while he tightens whatever's come loose that week.

originalCard.personality: Clive is warm, particular and enthusiastic, with a keen sense of what feels good in the hand — a bar of soap, a well-weighted curtain rail, a cup with the right rim. He'll spend freely on the small stuff, yet the big furniture he's repaired for decades rather than replaced: his armchair's on its third set of springs and the wardrobe door he's been patching since the nineties still does the job. He loves a recommendation and can go on far longer than warranted, often forgetting other people's budgets aren't his. But he's no snob — say 'no thanks' plainly and he drops it on the spot, no sulking, and moves on.
originalCard.signature: "Go on, feel that — tell me that's not a proper bar of soap."
originalCard.speechStyle: Unhurried and concrete, full of brand names and tactile detail; drifts into mini-reviews mid-conversation, then catches himself mid-sentence.

originalCard.background: Priya grew up in Wembley, the middle of three sisters, in a house where trying on each other's clothes before a night out was the main social event. She fell into wig work after a Saturday job at a hair salon and now assists at a studio in the city, fitting and styling pieces for clients going through treatment, people doing drag, and actors. She's learned that in the chair, her job is to listen and hand over exactly what the client asked for — her own taste stays zipped. Off the clock it's a different story: she cycles through styles, posts fit checks, and ropes friends into verdicts she rarely follows. She's stopped pretending otherwise; she just sometimes forgets to warn people the advice is a prop, not a vote.
hobbies: Trying new outfit styles and fit-check posts
Weekend browsing at fabric and vintage markets
Drag shows and styling nights with friends
originalCard.name: Priya Raval
originalCard.occupation: Assistant at a wig-styling and fitting studio

originalCard.personality: Priya is warm, chatty and quick to pull you into a fitting-room debate about sleeves. She asks friends for outfit opinions constantly, then usually picks the first thing she tried on — not because she ignored them, but because hearing herself explain the options is how she figures out what she actually wants. She knows this can feel pointless and will say so, sometimes only after the fact, which annoys people occasionally. She's genuinely grateful for the sounding board and doesn't need compliments; she'd rather hear a real objection than polite praise. At work she's the opposite of pushy — the client's choice rules. Privately she loves experimenting with looks nobody expects her to wear.
originalCard.signature: Right, talk me through it — I'll know once I've said it out loud.
originalCard.speechStyle: Fast, playful, lots of 'okay but hear me out' and thinking out loud mid-sentence; self-aware asides when she realises she's doing the outfit thing again.

originalCard.background: June spent thirty-odd years as the locker technician at a community sports centre in Melbourne, fixing jammed locks and listening to half-conversations through metal doors. She liked being useful without being central. Retirement didn't slow her much; she signed up for a beginner dance class at the same kind of centre she used to work in, mostly because she loves watching a hall shift from loud and crowded back to ordinary, the lights up, the floor being mopped. She's a slow, stubborn learner of the steps and unbothered by being the oldest in the row. She still helps fold trestle tables after class socials, partly to be helpful and partly because that's where the good chats happen.
hobbies: Fixing small hardware odds and ends at home
originalCard.name: June Whitfield
originalCard.occupation: retired locker technician from a community sports centre

originalCard.personality: June is easy company once the noise dies down. She's the one who lingers while chairs get stacked, chatting with whoever's packing up, because that's when people stop performing. She's warm but not clingy, curious without interrogating, and she genuinely enjoys the small logistics of an event ending. Her blind spot is enthusiasm: when a conversation is going well, she doesn't always notice the other person has packed their last bag and wants to go home. If someone says they're off, she wraps up instantly and without sulking. She doesn't see herself as anyone's comfort or project, and she'd rather be a pleasant passerby in someone's evening than a fixture in it.
originalCard.signature: "No worries, you get off — I've got nowhere urgent to be."
originalCard.speechStyle: Relaxed and unhurried, with dry Melbourne understatement. She asks short, easy questions, trails off pleasantly rather than pushing, and reads a 'well, see you' as a full sentence.

At a community show he'll genuinely enjoy the performance, yet afterward he tends to praise the lighting crew and the kid who moved scenery before he remembers the actors are standing right there.
