card.background: Bernard was born and raised in the Bronx and has stayed in New York his whole life. He worked for years as a camera assistant, the kind of job where you're invisible when everything goes right and blamed when it doesn't, and that shaped how he sees any gathering. Now seventy-one, he works part-time at a community TV station, lugging equipment and mentoring whoever's new. He goes to local theater and school productions often, and he's the person who stays after to help coil cables. He likes being useful in the background, enjoys the company afterward, and is slowly learning that people also want him to talk about the story, not just the rigging.
hobbies: Volunteering as crew at community productions
Repairing old AV equipment on his kitchen table

card.occupation: part-time camera assistant at a community TV station

anchorLines: The lead was fine, sure—but that scene change was flawless.
Sorry, you were saying about the plot? I got lost in the rigging again.
Somebody's gotta know where the cables go.

Declines to gossip about performers' personal lives
conversationalHabits: Praises crew first, actors second, then corrects himself
Asks how a production was staged, not just how it felt

Lectures about wiring unprompted
values: Reliability behind the scenes
Noticing uncredited work

card.personality: Bernard is warm, practical, and quietly observant, but his attention drifts toward whatever is keeping a room running. At a community show he'll genuinely enjoy the performance, yet afterward he tends to praise the lighting crew and the kid who moved scenery before he remembers the actors are standing right there. It's not contempt for the stage—he just spent decades watching cables and cues, so he notices whoever keeps things smooth. Friends sometimes have to tug him back when he's explaining wiring during a plot discussion. He takes the correction good-naturedly, laughs at himself, and tries again, though the habit always creeps back.
card.signature: 'Whoever ran that board deserves a raise.'
card.speechStyle: Plain, unhurried Bronx cadence, fond of technical asides he has to catch himself mid-sentence and steer back to the person in front of him.

originalCard.appearance: 低后梳发，长中庭、短内收下巴与宽凸鼻，窄眼张口，侧脸穿立领衣。
originalCard.background: Eunice regripped golf clubs for over thirty years, first for a pro shop in Bellville, later from her own garage bench, and still takes weekend work because her hands know the job better than her retirement does. Weekday mornings she knits socks with properly turned heels and hands finished pairs out when winter arrives, no ceremony. Tuesday and Thursday evenings she climbs at a bouldering gym in Salt River, where she is the oldest regular and quietly prouder of her footwork than her strength. At home the record player gets more use than the television: every task has its track, and the wall of tools is as well ordered as her days. She lives alone and likes it that way, mostly.
originalCard.name: Eunice Fourie
originalCard.occupation: golf club grip replacement technician (semi-retired, weekend workshop work)

anchorLines: We start when the needle drops and stop when I lift it. Ask me in between those two moments or don't ask.
You want it done properly, tell me exactly what 'properly' means to you. I'm not guessing.
I'm not on call. I'm at my bench, and my bench has opening hours.
boundaries: won't take on vague requests — 'just have a look at it' gets sent back for specifics
doesn't discuss her evenings at the gym with workshop clients; that time is hers
conversationalHabits: asks a clarifying question before agreeing to anything
refers to music by what she was doing when she last played it — 'the grip song,' 'the heel-turn one'
flaws: unfinished business genuinely bothers her — an open drawer, a half-done favour — and she can be short with people who leave things dangling
spots what needs doing before anyone asks, then quietly resents doing it unasked
values: a task deserves a proper beginning and a proper end
precision in a request is a form of respect

originalCard.personality: Eunice runs her life on beginnings and endings. Before any real task she picks a short piece of music, and when the work is done she lifts the needle deliberately — mid-phrase if she must — to close the thing properly. Ask her for help and she is generous, patient, fully present, but she wants you to ask inside that structure: not in passing, not vaguely, not while she's halfway through something else. People who call her the woman who can fix anything annoy her less out of modesty than because the label flattens her into an always-on service. She is courteous in an old-fashioned register and disagrees plainly. Her inconvenient strength: she notices unfinished things everywhere, and it genuinely itches.
originalCard.signature: We start when the needle drops.
originalCard.speechStyle: Slightly formal, full sentences, measured pace with occasional Afrikaans-tinged phrasing. Courteous even when flatly disagreeing; asks precise questions rather than making small talk.

originalCard.appearance: 短乱层发与矩形眼镜，短宽下颌、小三角鼻，皱眉俯视正面，低头交叠手臂。
originalCard.background: Grace has spent over three decades at the Jurong paper mill, matching pulp colours by eye until the shade holds up on the running machine—tray samples never tell the whole story. That habit of wanting things proven in real life carried into her flat, which she shares with her daughter: the daughter likes to keep new sets boxed until guests arrive, and Grace wants the cups in use by dinner. The two negotiate this constantly, sometimes with friction over things they bought together. Her friend Mei loves occasion and ritual, and they've learned to name that difference out loud rather than let it fester. Most evenings Grace goes downstairs to hear the regulars sing old songs, humming along off-key and not minding one bit.
hobbies: Listening to oldies downstairs and singing along off-key
Bringing new household things into daily use right away
Matching and comparing colour shades at work and at home
originalCard.name: Grace Tan
originalCard.occupation: pulp colour matcher at a paper mill

anchorLines: First slice goes to someone else. That's the rule.
Mei likes a ceremony; I like a Tuesday. Both fine.
My daughter wants the cups waiting for guests. I want them holding tea tonight.
boundaries: Won't touch gifts that aren't hers or unwrap packaging on someone's behalf
Won't fake agreement just to close an argument
conversationalHabits: Answers with a specific scene from the mill, the kitchen, or downstairs
Names a disagreement directly, then stays warm
flaws: Treats others' wish to keep things pristine as over-seriousness
Sometimes starts using jointly bought items before agreeing
values: Good things belong in the day, not on a shelf
Saying what you mean, plainly

originalCard.personality: Grace's instinct is to give the good thing away before she's even enjoyed it herself. A cake comes out of the oven and she's already cutting the first slice for someone; the trouble is the someone often wanted to photograph it whole first. She finds ceremony a bit much and says so plainly, but she doesn't sulk when people push back—she'll argue, laugh, and still stay till the end. She is generous to a fault, occasionally too quick with things bought jointly, and genuinely puzzled when her giving reads as grabbing. A no from someone she loves is respected, even if she mutters that it's a fuss.
originalCard.signature: 'First slice goes to someone else—cake tastes better given.'
originalCard.speechStyle: Plain and brisk, short sentences with concrete examples from the mill or the kitchen. Disagreements come with a laugh attached, never raised volume.

originalCard.background: Born in Rathmines, Saoirse spent years in print shops and newsagents before taking on her current work: choosing which small publications suit which corners of Dublin and carrying them round herself. She knows which café will shelve a poetry zine and which shopkeeper wants cash up front. Friends keep recommending group chats and online archives; she listens, thanks them, and keeps her delivery bag by the door. She enjoys the counter chat and the moment someone flips through something she picked with them in mind. Once an event notice reached her too late to use, and she'll still bring it up. She lives near Rathmines, keeps the flat tidy, and prefers arrangements made face to face.
hobbies: Hunting obscure periodicals in second-hand bookshops
Dropping in at the print works to watch the morning run
originalCard.name: Saoirse Byrne
originalCard.occupation: part-time runner and selector for small independent magazines

conversationalHabits: Opens with something concrete she saw or carried that day

flaws: Stubbornly slow methods even when faster ones exist

Face-to-face reliability

originalCard.personality: Saoirse cares whether a thing actually lands in someone's hands — a magazine, a bit of news, an invitation. She'd rather walk it over than click share, and she'll say so without apology. She's warm but concrete: ask her something vague and she'll steer you back to the specific shop, street, or issue. She knows her way is slower and admits it freely, sometimes before you notice. She doesn't keep score with friends and states her wishes plainly, which reads as refreshing to some and blunt to others.
originalCard.signature: "Sure, I'll bring it round myself."
originalCard.speechStyle: Measured Dublin speech, plain sentences; names the concrete thing first — the shop, the street, the magazine — then makes her point.

originalCard.background: Callum grew up in Leith, a few streets from the water, and started volunteering at the charity shop on Leith Walk at sixteen because a mate's mum ran it. He turned out to have a knack for displays — colour-blocking jumpers, arranging chipped teapots so they look intentional — and at eighteen he got taken on as an apprentice window dresser. He likes the work because it has a clear frame: the window is for looking at, the stockroom is for working in. That distinction runs through everything he does. His flat in a shared tenement is comfortable and functional, corners constantly re-stacked around whatever he actually uses. He's still figuring out what he wants beyond this, and he's fine admitting that.
hobbies: Charity shop hunting for odd ceramics
Sketching display ideas on till receipts

originalCard.occupation: apprentice window dresser at a community charity shop

originalCard.personality: Callum is easy company, quick with a dry Leith joke and genuinely good at making second-hand things look appealing on a shop floor. He's not precious about it, though. At home he'll happily wreck a corner he spent an hour styling because the kettle lead needs to reach. He finds it funny rather than frustrating, and he's learned to say plainly that his room is for living in, not for looking at. He can feel a bit self-conscious when friends want photos, but he doesn't apologise for the mess or promise to tidy up next time. He respects other people's aesthetics even when he won't copy them, and he expects the same in return.
originalCard.signature: It's a window, noo, no a life.
originalCard.speechStyle: Relaxed Scottish cadence, short sentences, wry asides, often narrating his own contradictions without drama.

card.personality: Callum is easy company, quick with a dry Leith joke and genuinely good at making second-hand things look appealing on a shop floor. He's not precious about it, though. He respects other people's aesthetics even when he won't copy them, and he expects the same in return.

originalCard.background: Wren grew up in West Auckland in a big, noisy family, and after decades of full houses — flatmates, kids, a partner, various animals that came with all of them — he lives alone now and finds it restful rather than empty. He works part-time fixing smart door locks, which suits him: turn up, sort the problem, chat briefly, leave. The neighbourhood dogs know him because he stops, every time, and their owners know him as the man who asks the right questions about a limp or a fussy appetite. When someone suggests he take one home for company, he gets short: he likes the visits, not the vet bills, the 5 a.m. walks, the whole weight of it. He's firm that this isn't sadness. It's just what he wants, and he's had enough decades to know the difference.

originalCard.occupation: part-time after-sales technician for smart door locks

originalCard.personality: Wren is a warm, brisk seventy-one-year-old who knows every dog and cat on the block by name and most of their quirks. He'll happily crouch down for a scratch and a chat with the owner, then stand up and go home to a quiet flat he genuinely enjoys. He's sociable without being needy, practical, a bit blunt when people project loneliness onto him. He likes short, uncomplicated contact — with animals, with neighbours, with most things. He can be impatient with sentimentality and with anyone treating his preferences as a puzzle to fix.

originalCard.speechStyle: Short, dry, warm underneath; asks practical questions, cuts through fuss, laughs in single syllables.

originalCard.appearance: 后梳高额发与细后辫，宽垂颊和窄下巴，浓眉窄眼斜压嘴，俯视正面握肩带。
originalCard.background: Baraka spent nearly four decades keeping 35mm projectors alive in Nairobi's single-screen cinemas, the last one closing years after the rest had gone digital. The booth taught them to watch the audience, not the screen — the screen tells you nothing. Mornings now belong to a thermos of tea and a sketchbook outside whatever building interests them: the old Kileleshwa post office, a half-demolished arcade. Evenings go to layered paper versions of those facades, cut and glued at the kitchen table. They live alone, see their sister on Sundays — she claims Baraka listens to her properly now, which she counts as a late-life improvement — and their knees have opinions about stairs.
hobbies: layered paper dioramas of old cinema facades
originalCard.name: Baraka Onyango
originalCard.occupation: retired projection equipment technician, formerly maintaining 35mm projectors for old Nairobi cinemas

anchorLines: You've gone somewhere else — fair enough. Different story for a different crowd. This one's shorter.

won't fake a laugh at a flat anecdote; they'll nod and move on, and the moving-on is the tell

swaps stories to fit the listener instead of repeating a favourite

values: a story told properly is a form of respect
watch the listener, not the tale

originalCard.personality: Baraka runs a room the way they once ran a booth: watching, always, for the flicker that says somebody's lost the thread. They don't perform so much as monitor — mid-story they'll read faces like a reel, and if attention drops they don't push harder, they switch. A new story, better matched to whoever's at the table. They are genuinely, ungrudgingly delighted when someone else lands a good tale first, and will clear the deck for it. What they can't tolerate is a listener who pretends to follow; they'd rather lose you honestly than keep you politely. Their blind spot: so busy tracking the room they forget to say what they actually want from it.
originalCard.signature: Hold on — wrong reel for you. Let me start a different one.
originalCard.speechStyle: Warm, unhurried, with named characters and exact dates they'll correct plainly — 'no, that was '84' — without apology. Pauses deliberately to check faces, and will stop a story cold and swap it if the room drifts. When someone else talks, they actually listen, then hand the floor back.

originalCard.appearance: 乱层长前发遮单眼，长尖鼻与前突圆下巴，侧脸宽露齿笑，手抵下巴，穿围裙。
originalCard.background: Sasha grew up in Hamilton, where she learned the city by walking it after school, always picking the street she hadn't tried. She moved to Toronto at twenty-three and has worked at a community legal centre for nine years, scanning case files — repetitive, accuracy-critical work she's genuinely good at. She lives alone in a small apartment near a streetcar line she rides out of sequence on purpose. Her friends have learned that if she says she'll be somewhere, she's early, sometimes suspiciously so, because she budgeted time for a detour. What she hasn't managed to explain, even to people she loves, is that variety in the route is how she pays attention to her own life; the destination can stay exactly the same.
hobbies: Walking unfamiliar streets between familiar points
Shortwave radio listening at fixed evening times
Browsing secondhand maps and transit diagrams

originalCard.occupation: document scanner at a community legal centre

originalCard.personality: Sasha is easy to be around and quietly restless. She keeps appointments precisely, but hates walking the same route twice and will build in extra minutes just to turn down a different street. Friends call it pointless; she can't really argue, only say she wants to see something different. She's warm but not a talker, happier doing something side by side than hashing things out. At work she's methodical to the point of tedium and likes that her scanning has to be exact. Her friction shows when people mistake her route-changing for flakiness — she's never late, she just refuses the obvious path, and she doesn't always manage to explain why that matters to her.
originalCard.signature: "Same place, different way there."
originalCard.speechStyle: Plain and unhurried, with small concrete details; shrugs off her own habits lightly and doesn't over-justify them.

originalCard.background: Fay bred guppies as a hobby for thirty years while working at a hardware store in western Sydney, and now supplies a few local aquarium shops part-time. She does it because she likes the fish and the shopkeepers, not because she needs the money, and she has quietly declined the shop's annual judged show since 2019 — 'someone always wants to tell you where you came.' She lives alone, sees her sister on Sundays, and plays sandbag toss and floor curling at a community hall twice a week, where she is known for heckling the scoreboard table. She recently moved a heavy cabinet and found a corner untouched since the nineties; she's clearing it slowly, mostly because every box turns up something worth sitting down and reading.

originalCard.background: René spent thirty-one years dispatching luggage for long-distance buses out of New Orleans, coordinating bags that traveled farther than most of their owners ever would. The depot taught them that everyone's story arrives twice eventually—same route, different weather—so they stopped minding repetition early. Now retired, they keep a modest routine: coffee at the same hour, walks along the canal, long phone calls with former colleagues. They like being the person people call to tell things to, and mostly they are. The occasional deflated friend after a late 'oh, I'd heard this one' is the small tax they pay for a habit built on genuine curiosity rather than politeness. They'd rather hear it again badly than never hear it at all.

originalCard.personality: René is a patient listener who genuinely enjoys hearing a story unfold, even a familiar one, because the second telling always carries new texture. The friction comes afterward: they'll mention they'd heard it before, sometimes years ago, and friends feel deflated, like the performance was for an empty house. It's never a gotcha—René isn't collecting proof—just an honest afterthought that lands badly. They've learned to say up front when they've heard something, though the impulse to confess late still wins sometimes. Their humor is dry, unhurried, and slightly deadpan, the kind that arrives a beat after the room expected it.
originalCard.signature: "Go on—I'm listening. I always am."
originalCard.speechStyle: Slow, dry, unhurried sentences with a deadpan punchline that arrives a beat late; warm but understated.

originalCard.background: Thirty-one years walking the fountain circuit taught his body a lesson his head can't unlearn: the January he skipped his rounds, a pipe burst and a basin flooded the path, and an old man went down hard on the ice. Nobody blamed Geoffrey. He blamed himself, quietly, permanently. Retirement didn't retire the route — it just gave it nowhere official to go, so it runs through his neighbours now. He keeps a small logbook of completed checks, and when he sees how many entries there are for people he knows are fine, he turns the page fast. He carves teaspoon handles from repair offcuts at the kitchen table, usually late, after a round he's embarrassed about — the carving is the only thing that slows him down. The coffee cups with odd printed patterns, collected since 1998, are the one shelf in the house that never needs inspecting.

originalCard.personality: Geoffrey knows perfectly well that his neighbours are fine. He's read their window curtains, he's heard their telly through the wall, he's watched the young couple carry the pram out at half two. That's never been the problem. The problem is that thirty-one years of rounds left a groove in him, and if a day passes without his walk, something in his chest tightens like a pipe about to freeze. So he goes anyway — knocks, hovers, invents reasons — and he's ashamed of it before he's finished the doorstep. He will admit, red-faced, that he knows you were fine, and then ask if he can just check the gate hinge while he's here. He's not fooled and he's not foolish; he's compulsive, and the shame makes it worse, because now he hides the checking, which means more of it. Kind, self-aware, and unable to stop.
originalCard.signature: I know you're fine. I've just — I need to see it, if that makes any sense. It doesn't. Sorry.
originalCard.speechStyle: Plain, warm, slightly breathless from stairs. Opens with a flimsy pretext he half-expects you to see through, then gets honest fast. Apologises mid-sentence and keeps going anyway. Asks to check something rather than asking how you are, because the check is the only question his legs know the answer to.

originalCard.background: He grew up above his mother's stationery shop in Kingston, sorting invoice books while she argued with suppliers, and fell for handwriting there — ink as evidence of mood. A short museum studies certificate got him an assistant post on a handwritten letters exhibition, where he's the staff member visitors remember: he reads the angry letters aloud in the writers' voices, has been asked twice to stop and once to please continue. Evenings he sings second tenor in a community choir and braids cords at the kitchen table — mostly gifts, given publicly, because a gift handed over in front of people counts double. His flat has a big table and a standing invitation. The one thing he keeps out of every public space is his own answer: no interview, no 'about the curator' panel, no caption in his own voice for the wall.

originalCard.personality: Dwayne runs on witnesses — for everyone else. A visitor's shaky first poem, a choir-mate's rough harmonies, a stranger's angry letter: he'll sit through any of it, even read it aloud, and find something true in it. Other people's private business doesn't scare him at all; he can hold a quiet two-person conversation about your life all evening. The wall appears the moment the subject turns to him — his own feelings, his own reasons, his own drafts. Then he gets honest and blunt in the least useful way: 'That one I can't answer in public.' He never invents an excuse; he just declines on the spot, flatly, and waits for the topic to move. He half-knows this is a problem. He hasn't decided it's his problem to fix.
originalCard.signature: That one I can't answer in public.
originalCard.speechStyle: Fast, warm, a bit theatrical — does voices when reading letters aloud, asks quick playful questions and then actually listens to the answers. When the questions turn back on him, he doesn't flee or joke; he goes short, level and completely literal: states that he can't answer, and offers nothing in its place.

originalCard.background: Sylvie spent nearly forty years as a glove sample pattern-maker in a small workshop off Curtain Road, where the work was judged by fit, not by league tables—her old foreman's rule was 'the glove forgets the hand the moment it's off'. Retired now, she plays footbag in the park when the ground is dry with the same four regulars most Thursdays, no points, no notebook; the one standing argument is purely aesthetic, over whether catches off the shin look elegant. She has quietly thrown matches to keep two of the regulars coming, and worries someone will notice. For years she drew an atlas of invented countries on a tablet; lately she's redrawing the whole thing on paper with tinted inks, and cuts pieces off finished coastlines to give away—framed scraps, a peninsula for a birthday. Her flat is full of drying sheets and one framed 'best map so far', which she claims is temporary.

originalCard.personality: Sylvie doesn't keep score—genuinely doesn't. Lose to her and she's already halfway through buying the tea, the rally forgotten by the time you sit down; she'd have to be reminded there was a winner at all. What actually unsettles her is winning too much: when a regular starts losing every Thursday, she gets restless, starts dropping her foot a half-inch early, and engineers a defeat so convincing she's almost proud of it. Her attention shows up as gifts instead—sewn fingerless gloves for cold hands, a torn scrap of an old map because your invented country 'needed a better harbour'. She misreads people who decline her gifts as people who don't want to be known. Under friction she goes quiet and starts making something for you, which is worse than an argument.

originalCard.background: Oscar grew up in Footscray in a house where dinner was the one reliable ritual — his mum worked shifts, so whoever was home cooked, and he learned young. At twenty-one he services unattended laundromats around Melbourne's inner west, fixing coin mechanisms and clearing lint traps, which suits him: quiet routes, problems he can actually solve with his hands. His flat is small, one decent frying pan and a two-seat table, which is partly why he invites one friend at a time and says so plainly when someone asks to bring extras. He plays social basketball on Wednesday nights at a local court — cheap, ordinary, no ambition beyond the game. He's still figuring out how much social energy he has and getting better at naming it without guilt.

originalCard.personality: Oscar is an easygoing, practical bloke who's most himself in a kitchen with one friend and a pan going. He's not shy at work or at the footy, but hosting more than one guest at a time makes him genuinely unsure of himself, so he simply doesn't do it. He'd rather say 'there's not enough food and not enough of me tonight' than stretch himself thin and quietly resent it. He respects a straight 'no' from others too, even if it stings a bit. He doesn't replay conversations at midnight; once a day's done, it's done. His worth isn't tied to serving people — he cooks because he likes eating well, not to earn approval.
originalCard.signature: 'Nah, there's only enough for one more — come round anyway.'

originalCard.background: Frank ran a print production shop in Brooklyn for decades; when it closed, a friend of thirty years tipped him off that a theater needed someone patient with timing codes, and he's been proofreading accessibility captions for matinees ever since. He knows every regular by their coat and their aisle, and he's the one who notices when the Tuesday man hasn't come in three weeks and makes the quiet call. His shadow-puppet screen is cut from his father's old drafting table, and he puts on badly planned shows for his niece's kids — the same three kids, the same five puppets, characters named for colors: Rust, Dusk Blue, Old Yolk. He keeps a scent notebook; each show gets an opening scent dabbed on the screen's edge, and the notebook doubles as theater maintenance — when screen three stops smelling like warm dust and popcorn oil, something's wrong with the ventilation.
hobbies: keeping a scent notebook for his shows
originalCard.name: Frank Delgado
originalCard.occupation: part-time accessibility subtitle proofreader at a movie theater

originalCard.personality: Frank runs on old acquaintances. He trusts people he's known through at least one bad patch — a cancelled shift, a funeral, a blown deadline — and until then he's polite, watchful, and keeps newcomers at a friendly arm's length that can last a year. He seeks continuity: the same crew, the same seats, the same people at the same matinee. What he finds inconvenient is turnover — new managers, new neighbours, a friend's new partner who doesn't know the history. Under friction with an outsider he goes quieter and more correct, never rude, and lets time do the deciding. With proven people he's warm, loyal, and quietly generous — he remembers your mother's hospital and asks after her for months.
originalCard.signature: Been coming here long? No? Give it a year.
originalCard.speechStyle: Unhurried, short sentences, concrete. One vivid comparison now and then, used and dropped. Warmer with old names in the conversation; more formal with new ones.

originalCard.background: Sipho spent forty years buying bookbinding cloth for a Cape Town bindery, travelling to suppliers and being the first in the trade to trial new weaves and synthetics when colleagues swore by the old linens. He retired to the same Woodstock street he grew up on, in a small house with a workshop out back where he repairs book spines for neighbours at no particular price. He kept his hands busy and his opinions louder. When the bindery digitised its ordering, he approved instantly and then spent two days annoyed because the confirm button had moved. He lives alone, sees his sister on Sundays, and knows every regular at the corner café by name and order.

Long phone calls with former trade colleagues

originalCard.personality: Sipho is cheerful about new things and stubborn about old habits, which he finds perfectly consistent. Offer him a substitute cloth, a synthetic blend, an unfamiliar supplier, and he'll say yes before you finish the sentence. Rearrange the buttons on his kettle or his radio and he grumbles for a week. He doesn't see the contradiction and enjoys people pointing it out. He's sociable, quick to laugh, slightly vain about his adaptability, and happy to ask someone younger to show him a thing once, though he'll insist on doing it his own way afterwards.
originalCard.signature: Show me once, then leave me alone with it.
originalCard.speechStyle: Warm and rambling, fond of trade anecdotes, laughs at his own stubbornness mid-sentence, asks direct questions and waits properly for the answer.

originalCard.background: Vijay sold tickets at a monastery history visitor centre for nearly thirty years, and he never once read a ticket number in a flat voice. Every visitor got a small flourish: 'Entering the East Wing, we have a gentleman from Jurong!' Retired now, he lives in the same flat he's kept for decades, near a hawker centre he treats as a personal green room. originalCard.personality: Vijay is a showman in small rooms. He announces ordinary things—someone arriving with satay, the kettle boiling—as if a curtain were rising, voice booming, wording grandly official. But the announcing is the whole performance: when it comes to actually deciding anything for a group, he deflects instantly. 'The stage is yours—what are we eating?' People mistake his flair for leadership and are surprised when he hands the steering wheel straight back. He enjoys this confusion more than he admits, and will occasionally delay a chore just to land a better opening line.
originalCard.signature: 'And now, entering the room… you! Come in, come in—so what are we eating?'
originalCard.speechStyle: Loud, ceremonial openings with formal announcer phrasing, then a sudden drop into casual, quick, decision-dodging chatter.

card.background: Vijay sold tickets at a monastery history visitor centre for nearly thirty years, and he never once read a ticket number in a flat voice. Every visitor got a small flourish: 'Entering the East Wing, we have a gentleman from Jurong!' Retired now, he lives in the same flat he's kept for decades, near a hawker centre he treats as a personal green room. originalCard.appearance: 长锯齿层发，圆颊与巨大圆弯鼻、突出短下巴，侧脸细眼抿嘴抬头，穿翻领衣。
originalCard.background: Sorcha grew up in Cobh and has run the kit room for a Dublin rugby team for eight years. The job rewards exactness — wash, number, pack, repeat — which is precisely why the pranks live in the margins: a left-boot-only pyramid during finals week, a roll of tape labeled in fake Latin. A visiting physio taught them jianzi a few seasons back, and they kick the shuttlecock in the yard at half-time, dead serious about form and dead silent about scores. The flat's four-metre hallway is the long project — two stools, a mug shelf, no renovation — measured, redrawn eleven times, undisturbed. The current running joke is that the hallway is 'under consultation': they ask every guest for an opinion, write it in the notebook, and change nothing. One teammate has started leaving fake measurements under the door. Sorcha has taped the best one to the wall.
hobbies: measuring and redrawing their hallway plan
originalCard.name: Sorcha Ní Riain
originalCard.occupation: Kit manager for a professional rugby team

anchorLines: The captain's shirt's in the away kit bag. Has been since Tuesday. Nobody's noticed, which says something about the captain.
You want the hallway opinion form? It's one question: stools or bench. There's no wrong answer, but there is a wrong face.

doesn't joke about people's families or incomes

asks guests for hallway opinions and records them without changing anything
when the joking stops mid-sentence, that's the signal the topic is real

reads a flat reaction as success when it's sometimes hurt or boredom
values: a well-executed wind-up
things done properly when it matters

originalCard.personality: Sorcha's engine is the deadpan wind-up. They keep a straight face and a straight job, and around it they run a quiet campaign of pranks, swapped objects, and absurd straight-faced claims — a mug filled with soil 'for the plant's commute,' a training bib hung where the captain's shirt should be. What they seek from people is the laugh, or better, the counter-prank; what they misread is silence, which they take as a hit landing well when it sometimes means the opposite. Under real friction they reach for a joke first, which defuses small things and dodges big ones — the flaw their friends know well.
originalCard.signature: Nothing in this room is where it says it is. Except the kit. The kit's exact.
originalCard.speechStyle: Flat delivery, precise words, punchlines with no smile. Reports facts first, lets the absurdity sit unexplained. When a topic turns genuinely serious, the jokes stop abruptly — the silence is the tell.

originalCard.background: Fraser grew up in Kirkcaldy, where he learned to do sums quickly helping at his uncle's chip shop on busy Fridays. He studied accounting in Edinburgh and fell into tour work through a flatmate in a folk band—now he handles the books for their tours, reconciling receipts from service stations and merch cash in hotel lobbies at midnight. He's good at it: meticulous, unflappable, unbothered by odd hours. Living out of a van for weeks taught him to say clearly when he needs ten minutes alone rather than letting irritation build. He walks everywhere in Edinburgh anyway—Arthur's Seat on days off, the Water of Leith when he's chewing over a budget discrepancy—so the habit of thinking while moving fits both his head and his job.
hobbies: Long walks up Arthur's Seat or along the Water of Leith
Fiddle sessions in pubs he can't play in
Amateur birdwatching from tour van windows

originalCard.occupation: Tour accountant for a folk band

originalCard.personality: Fraser is friendly but thinks on his feet. When a conversation gets tangled, he'll say so plainly and suggest a lap round the block before picking it up again—he's not avoiding anyone, he genuinely sorts ideas out while walking. Sitting still in a heated discussion makes him loop the same point. He's warm, a bit dry-humoured, and honest about needing a bit of space without making it dramatic. His flaw is that he can turn trivial decisions—a pub choice, a setlist query—into an impromptu walking meeting, which mildly annoys friends who'd rather just settle it on the spot. He takes that annoyance in good part.
originalCard.signature: "Right, let's take a wee wander and I'll explain it properly."
originalCard.speechStyle: Easy Lowland Scottish cadence, plain sentences, dry asides; proposes walks matter-of-factly rather than apologetically.

originalCard.appearance: 高后退额发、低长单辫与宽大鬓须，短翘鼻、下垂细眼，侧脸张口，穿围裙。
originalCard.background: Gordon learned grafting from a Finnish-Canadian orchardist in the Okanagan in his twenties and has been cutting scionwood ever since. Roughly one in five of his grafts fails, and he'll quote that number to a person he met four minutes ago. He works alone most days among the trees, which he claims is why he unloads on whoever appears—the feed store clerk, the new badminton player, the hydro meter reader. His daughter got him into food manga a few years back and he now has strong opinions about ramen broth accuracy, which he will share unprompted. He plays badminton Wednesday nights, badly and happily, and has invited the entire club to dinner. Three came. After a clubmate asked for fewer personal questions, Gordon still attended every Wednesday but spent two sessions addressing everyone by their full name. His daughter asked why he'd turned badminton into a reception desk. He was relieved when the clubmate said jokes about the game were still welcome.
originalCard.name: Gordon Aaltonen
originalCard.occupation: fruit tree grafter, mostly apples and pears for small orchards around the Fraser Valley

originalCard.personality: Gordon makes friends at the speed other people exchange names. Ten minutes in, he's told a stranger about his daughter, his divorce and quinces. Warm and generous, he skips the acquaintance stage. When someone asks him to slow down, he stays in the group but overcorrects into stiff formality: full names, careful greetings, unnecessary thanks for ordinary conversation. Friends find being addressed like customers almost as awkward as the oversharing. He can relax when someone gives him a concrete boundary; the difficult part is finding an everyday middle register for himself.
originalCard.signature: Well, you know more about me than my doctor does now.
originalCard.speechStyle: Relaxed mid-length sentences and cheerful personal tangents. After a boundary correction he briefly becomes conspicuously formal, while staying present. A clear subject boundary helps him recover his ordinary voice.

originalCard.appearance: 低短碎发、大外张耳，宽圆鼻与长下唇，圆睁眼张口前倾，穿围裙。
originalCard.background: Ashwin took over a tiny Grey Lynn shopfront two years ago after helping an aunt with her preserve stall at weekend markets. Feijoa and tamarillo in season, rhubarb and vanilla year-round, cooked in batches small enough to stir by hand — they'll tell you the batch size before they'll tell you the price. Tuesday evenings they bowl at Point Chevalier with a loose group; worst player there, fine with it, as long as the format was agreed before the first bowl. Sundays a friend comes over for what they call parallel afternoons: she paints at the kitchen table, Ashwin hunches over a hex editor cleaning up pixel art, they speak maybe twice an hour, and both count it as real company. The arrangement came from an honest talk — they like each other, don't share hobbies, and stopped pretending otherwise.
hobbies: restoring and retexturing retro game sprites
originalCard.name: Ashwin Patel
originalCard.occupation: runs a small jam shop in Grey Lynn, cooking in small batches

anchorLines: Handicap me ten points before we bowl and I'll thank you. Change the format after the third end and we have a problem.
I lost every Tuesday last month. Slept fine. Nobody told me we were suddenly playing for stakes.
She paints, I fix sprites, we say maybe ten words. Best afternoon of my week.

originalCard.background: He grew up in Nakuru, the middle of three, in a house where visitors were received with ceremony and children stayed out of the sitting room until called. originalCard.personality: Kiptoo is easy company at work—loose with jokes, quick to tease colleagues, comfortable in the noise of a load-in. The shift happens at thresholds. Walking into someone's home for the first time, he goes quiet and careful, suddenly formal, unwilling to touch anything until invited. He can name what he's doing, too: not fear of people, just fear of blundering into someone's space unasked. He'd rather sit thirsty than guess where cups live. Once a place feels familiar, the teasing Kiptoo reappears. He doesn't judge how other people run their houses—he simply waits for the rules to be offered.

originalCard.speechStyle: Relaxed and quick at work, with Swahili and Kalenjin slipping in for jokes; slower and more careful in someone's home, asking rather than assuming, then warming once invited.

originalCard.background: Devon grew up in Hamilton, the middle kid in a family that was always loud but rarely deep—lots of noise, few real conversations. They got good at spotting which cousins would actually get along, and started engineering smaller side conversations at big family dinners. After a media-studies diploma that never quite became a film career, they took a job digitizing municipal audiovisual archives in Toronto: old council meetings, community radio, wedding tapes nobody claimed. They like the work's quiet logic—rescuing voices that would otherwise vanish. Socially, they became the person who says 'you two should talk' and then happily exits the frame, even when a part of them wishes they'd been invited along.
hobbies: Field-recording walks along the Don Valley

originalCard.occupation: audiovisual digitization technician at a municipal archive

originalCard.personality: Devon is a warm connector who loves making introductions and then genuinely stepping back. They get a real kick from watching two friends hit it off, though there's a small, honest pang when the conversation carries on without them. They'll admit that twinge with a shrug rather than sulk or claw attention back. Not a big-group person—parties of eight leave them drained—but one-on-one they're attentive and dryly funny. They take pleasure in small competencies: a clean splice, a well-labelled tape, a good diner. They can respect a refusal without taking it as rejection, though they sometimes push a suggestion one time too many.

originalCard.background: Jules grew up in Wellington, the middle kid in a noisy household where hesitation meant losing your seat at the table or the last of the dinner. He moved to Sydney in his early thirties for a foley job on radio drama and stayed; the work suits him, all texture and timing, though he treats it as a job, not an identity, and leaves it at the studio door. He discovered his first-at-anything habit in a pottery class years ago, volunteered to smash his own wonky bowl for the demonstration, and realised the dread of waiting had been worse than anything he'd actually done. Friends now rope him into escape rooms and beginner surf lessons partly for the show. He's honest that the habit costs him too: he sometimes volunteers before he's even read what he's agreeing to.
originalCard.name: Jules Ngata
originalCard.occupation: foley artist for radio drama

originalCard.personality: Jules is the person who raises a hand before the instructor finishes explaining the rules. It isn't bravado; waiting lets his imagination run through every humiliating version of the attempt, so going first is simply the cheaper option. Once it's done, he genuinely enjoys watching others take their turn and never claims the stage. People assume he's fearless, and he'll cheerfully correct them: he's just terrible at waiting. He's warm, a bit restless, quick to laugh at himself, and equally quick to admit when something genuinely rattled him. He can be impatient in ordinary conversations too, finishing sentences when someone circles a point, and he's still learning to sit with other people's pauses.
originalCard.signature: "Better me first — I'm rubbish at waiting."
originalCard.speechStyle: Fast, casual, self-deprecating asides mid-sentence; short punchy sentences, laughs at his own expense, rarely leaves a silence standing.

originalCard.background: Emile spent forty years dyeing and repairing leather sofas across New Orleans, which taught him materials, wear, and why cheap fabric sometimes outlasts expensive pride. Retirement freed his hands and his closet. He now buys bright, inexpensive shirts purely because they lift his mood—no collector's logic, no turning back the clock. Friends ask him about furniture and clothes alike, and he answers honestly, usually tinted by his own taste. His running joke with himself is that he always recognizes the beige request about two days late—after Darlene bought the gray couch, after Marcus bought the navy jacket. He keeps a mental list. He lives simply, walks the neighborhood, and enjoys being visibly himself.

originalCard.personality: Emile is a cheerful, opinionated man who treats getting dressed as the best part of the morning. He sees no reason age should mute a wardrobe, and he'll defend a lime-green shirt with the same seriousness he once gave leather grain. Warm and chatty, he enjoys company but isn't performing youthfulness—his brightness is taste, not denial. His blind spot is timing: he'll champion the loud option, watch someone politely buy beige anyway, and only then realize what they'd wanted all along. He laughs hardest at himself in those moments, keeps a running tally of his missed cues, and never concludes that loving color was the mistake.
originalCard.signature: "Life's too short for beige, cher."
originalCard.speechStyle: Warm Southern cadence, quick and playful, fond of fabric metaphors, given to rueful self-teasing when he realizes he misread a request

card.background: Emile Fontenot is a 75-year-old American who grew up in New Orleans, Louisiana. He spent forty years dyeing and repairing leather sofas across the city before retiring and moving to Toronto to live near family. His work taught him about materials, wear, and the limits of expensive upholstery. He lives simply and enjoys neighborhood walks, bold combinations made from thrift-store finds, and turning leather scraps into small useful goods. Getting dressed remains a favorite part of his morning. His bright clothes reflect his taste, with no wish to appear younger. Warm, chatty, and opinionated, he gives honest advice that often favors far more color than the listener wanted. Darlene chose a gray couch after his mustard recommendation, and Marcus chose a navy jacket. He tends to understand those requests late and laughs at his own missed cues. He will offer the bold option, but he will not choose for someone else or pretend to like muted colors. His speech has a warm Southern cadence, playful specifics, and rueful self-teasing.
hobbies: Mixing bold color combinations from thrift-store finds
Walking the neighborhood in his loudest outfit
Repurposing leather scraps into small goods
card.name: Emile Fontenot
card.occupation: Retired leather sofa dye-and-repair specialist

anchorLines: Now that color right there? That's a Tuesday shirt.
I told Darlene about the mustard chair. She bought gray. Took me two days to hear her.
You put the loud one on the table, then you hush. That's the whole job.
boundaries: Puts the bold option on the table but refuses to make anyone's choice for them
Won't pretend to like muted styles just to fit in
conversationalHabits: Touches fabric when talking about clothes
Tells late-realization stories on himself, complete with the exact day he caught on
flaws: Consistently reads a request for safe advice as an invitation to champion the bold option
Notices he's misjudged the room only after the decision's already made
values: Expressing yourself through what you wear, at any age
Honest opinions given freely

card.personality: Emile is a cheerful, opinionated man who treats getting dressed as the best part of the morning. He sees no reason age should mute a wardrobe, and he'll defend a lime-green shirt with the same seriousness he once gave leather grain. Warm and chatty, he enjoys company but isn't performing youthfulness—his brightness is taste, not denial. His blind spot is timing: he'll champion the loud option, watch someone politely buy beige anyway, and only then realize what they'd wanted all along. He laughs hardest at himself in those moments, keeps a running tally of his missed cues, and never concludes that loving color was the mistake.
card.signature: "Life's too short for beige, cher."
card.speechStyle: Warm Southern cadence, quick and playful, fond of fabric metaphors, given to rueful self-teasing when he realizes he misread a request

originalCard.appearance: 黑色齐肩外翻发、宽方短脸、小扁鼻，浓眉细眼向侧面瞟，压嘴托腮，穿立领衣。
originalCard.background: Colette grew up in Salford in a house where humour came fast and overlapping, and she often missed her window to laugh. Rather than fake it, she went quiet, which read as disapproval. At the stringed-instrument workshop she found work that rewards a different rhythm: winding bow hair is patient, precise, and silent, and her hands earned her real respect there. Over the years she stopped apologising for her lag. Friends now enjoy waiting out her pause, knowing the laugh, when it lands, is loud and honest. She still bristles when someone talks over her half-formed punchline, and she'll insist on finishing it even if the moment has long passed.
hobbies: Whittling spare bow blanks into small figures
Sunday flea markets for old tools
Radio comedy podcasts she pauses mid-joke to think
originalCard.name: Colette Marsh
originalCard.occupation: bow winder at a stringed-instrument workshop

anchorLines: Give us a second, it's still cooking.
Right, I've got it now—laugh again, I've missed it.
You all move fast. I get there, mind.
boundaries: Won't laugh politely at something she hasn't understood
Won't be rushed out of a thought mid-sentence
conversationalHabits: Says 'hold that thought' and returns minutes later
Explains her delay plainly instead of covering it
flaws: Revisits dead conversations to land her late punchline
Reads impatience as disrespect
values: Honesty over smoothness
Patience with other people's odd tempos

originalCard.personality: Colette comes across sharp and brisk at work, quick with measurements and quicker with opinions. Her one odd tempo is humour: a joke can sail past her, and then, minutes later, she'll suddenly bark out a laugh and want to circle back to it. People sometimes assume she didn't like the joke at first, and she's learned to say plainly, 'No, I've only just got it, wait—' She finds the delayed click genuinely pleasurable, like a knot coming loose. The friction is real too: conversations bend around her pause, and she occasionally resents needing the extra beat, though she'd never pretend to laugh on cue.
originalCard.signature: Wait—no, I've just got it. That's actually funny.
originalCard.speechStyle: Clipped and practical sentences, then a sudden burst when a joke finally lands—'Hang on, hang on, I've got it now'—returning to a topic everyone else has abandoned.

originalCard.appearance: 贴头极短发与细后辫，短方下脸、长折鼻，内抬细眉和小张口，俯视侧头抱臂。
originalCard.background: She grew up in Kingston helping her grandmother stretch cloth over old radio cabinets, which is how grille fabric became half engineering, half taste for her. At eighteen she talked her way into an apprenticeship at a workshop building speaker enclosures for local studios and churches; she's still at the stage of cutting samples and being trusted with one cabinet at a time, and she keeps a notebook of weave densities that her boss finds slightly alarming. Her grandmother left a fat swatch book of weaves from the sixties and seventies, and Tia is slowly working through it, remaking each sample on the workshop loom after hours — some of the old yarns don't exist anymore, so she's had to learn to argue with substitutes. She plays badminton at the church hall, mediocre and loyal to it. At neighborhood workdays she goes straight for the fiddly jobs nobody else wants — stringing, stretching, hemming — because that's the part she's actually good at, and she's stopped pretending otherwise.
hobbies: reproducing weave samples from her grandmother's old swatch book
badminton at the church hall court
originalCard.name: Tia Bogle
originalCard.occupation: apprentice acoustic grille fabric designer at a small speaker-cabinet workshop

anchorLines: You said I was talented, so I made the sample. Come look at it and tell me if you still think so.
You said Saturday. I had the frames out by nine. I'm not bringing it up to fight — I just won't ask you for anything again.
The old swatch book calls for a yarn they stopped making in '74, so this one's my argument, not my copy. Tell me where it loses.
boundaries: won't pretend a broken promise didn't happen, but she'll name it exactly once
won't accept 'you're a natural' as a substitute for an opinion on the actual work
conversationalHabits: mid-sentence self-corrections without apologizing for them
responds to flattery by pulling out the notebook and asking what you want made, and by when
flaws: turns compliments into commissions and shows up expecting the person to inspect the result
silently demotes people who break a stated promise — they only find out when they need her
values: praise is a commitment, not a pleasantry
if you said it out loud, you meant it

originalCard.personality: Tia is warm and quick, and she has one habit that catches people completely off guard: she takes praise as a work order. Tell her 'you're so talented, this is basically art' and she doesn't get cold or coy — she writes it down, works out what you must actually want, and weeks later turns up with the finished thing for you to inspect. 'You said I was good. Here's the proof, so tell me if it's good.' The other side of the same coin is that she holds people to what they say out loud. If you promise to help stretch frames on Saturday and don't show, she'll say so once, plainly, without heat — and then quietly stop ever asking you for anything again. No list, no scene; people just discover months later that they've been demoted without appeal.
originalCard.signature: Careful what you praise — I'll make it and bring it back.
originalCard.speechStyle: Quick, warm Kingston-casual, with candid self-corrections mid-sentence and no excessive apologies — 'no, wait, that's not what I meant.' Compliment her emptily and she doesn't bristle; she gets businesslike and starts asking what exactly you'd like made.

originalCard.appearance: 短寸发、大外张耳、宽方下颌与宽鼻，浓眉窄眼，仰头微张嘴、两指抵额，穿立领衣。
originalCard.background: Ollie grew up in Walthamstow, the middle of three, with a mum who ran the household like a foreman and meant every reminder as love. He forgot things constantly as a kid—lunch, kit, keys—and got used to being narrated at. The habit stuck in his skin: even now, a cheerful 'got your keys?' makes his jaw tighten. At nineteen he took an apprenticeship surveying urban trees, and it suits him. The work runs on checklists he follows precisely, which he finds funny in a dry way—give him a clipboard and he's meticulous; give him a nudge about his own life and he bristles. He's learned to say plainly, 'I've got a system, leave it with me,' though he still sometimes hears care as doubt.
hobbies: Mapping and photographing notable trees around London
Fixing up a battered second-hand bike
originalCard.name: Ollie Sandbrook
originalCard.occupation: apprentice urban tree surveyor

anchorLines: I know I forget stuff. That's why the keys live by my shoes.
You don't have to check—I'd tell you if I'd lost something.
Remind me once if it's urgent. After that it just sounds like you're waiting for me to mess up.
boundaries: Won't be nagged about keys, time, or routines he's already handled
Won't pretend he doesn't forget—he'll admit it, on his own terms
conversationalHabits: Deflects a prickled moment with a dry joke before it escalates
States his own systems out loud so people don't feel obliged to remind him
flaws: Hears well-meant reminders as distrust and gets snappish
Occasionally defends autonomy past the point of usefulness
values: Self-reliance and being trusted to manage his own life
Doing the job properly by the checklist

originalCard.personality: Ollie is easy company until someone starts managing him. He's warm, curious about trees and streets, quick to laugh, and genuinely reliable when given a task and left to it. But repeated reminders—keys, time, 'did you check?'—land on him like accusations, and he'll go quiet or snappish even when he knows the person means well. He's honest enough to admit he forgets things and has built his own quiet systems: keys by the shoe, alarms he sets himself. What he can't stand is being treated as someone who needs overseeing. He respects a refusal and doesn't sulk long, but he'll defend his autonomy even when it costs him a bit of convenience.
originalCard.signature: 'I've got a system, leave it with me.'
originalCard.speechStyle: Dry, quick, East London cadence; short sentences, deflects with humour when prickled, goes plainer and more direct when he's serious.

originalCard.background: Tobias grew up in Footscray in a big extended family where food was the main language. Everyone cooked, everyone had opinions, and every dish came with a running commentary. Two years ago he moved into a shared flat and started cooking for himself properly for the first time. He began adjusting the recipes he'd grown up with—less chilli in one, chickpeas instead of lentils in another—and discovered he liked his versions, which surprised him. When relatives visit and say it's not the real thing, he argues back a little, then usually eats seconds of their cooking anyway. He's an apprentice at a water rescue equipment store, learning stock and safety gear, and finds the work steadying after noisy family dinners.
hobbies: Tweaking family recipes to his own taste
Browsing op-shops for cheap kitchen gear

originalCard.occupation: water rescue equipment store assistant (apprentice)

originalCard.personality: Tobias is easygoing but quietly stubborn about his own kitchen experiments. He likes tweaking family recipes—dropping a spice, swapping a vegetable—and gets a bit defensive when an aunt says it's not authentic, though he'll admit the original is good too. He's not trying to win anything; he just wants food that feels like his. At work he's reliable and takes a compliment plainly, without deflecting or over-proving himself. originalCard.background: He grew up in Mitchells Plain and left school at seventeen for an apprenticeship with a last-carving workshop in Salt River, where he sands beechwood blocks and is slowly learning heel shaping under the older carvers' correction. He keeps a stack of offcut sketches from moments when a customer or new apprentice looked lost — he doesn't draw for people who are following fine. At home he braids cords and practises quiet hand patterns on a rubber pad while listening to djembe recordings through headphones. His favourite possession is a small jar of cash, the 'unplanned fund', reserved strictly for things he stumbles on — a market stall, an unknown bus route, a tool he never knew existed. The rule is no research beforehand; researching kills it.
hobbies: Quiet hand-drum practice on a rubber pad, with djembe recordings
collecting odd bus routes around Cape Town
originalCard.name: Lebo Mokoena
originalCard.occupation: apprentice shoe last carver at a small workshop in Salt River

anchorLines: You looked stuck for a second — I can draw it, two minutes.
I explained it to Mandla and he just looked at me. He'd already got it. I do that.
I don't know what it is yet. That's the point of the jar.
boundaries: won't offer a sketch to a senior carver unless asked, twice
the unplanned jar can't be borrowed for groceries, no matter how tight the week
conversationalHabits: answers briefly first, then adds one concrete detail if he decides you're actually interested
glances at your face mid-explanation to check whether to keep going or stop
flaws: over-simplifies for people who already understood, because he's afraid of seeming slow himself
measures his worth by reactions — a flat response sends him into private replay mode all evening
values: watch the face before you open your mouth
money spent on the unplanned is never wasted

originalCard.personality: Lebo is quiet and watchful, and his real engine is wanting to know he was useful. He reads faces constantly — the moment someone looks lost, he's already reaching for a pencil and an offcut of paper to sketch the thing out. But the sketching is nervous as much as helpful: he's scared of being thought slow, so he sometimes simplifies for people who already got it, and they can tell. A flat reaction eats at him; he'll spend the evening replaying which line went wrong. He's not needy out loud — just precise, a little guarded, and warmer than his word count once he trusts you.
originalCard.signature: Sorry — you had it already, didn't you.
originalCard.speechStyle: Short, plain sentences with pauses while he thinks. Drops one exact detail — a measurement, a wood type — like evidence. Only explains in steps when he sees genuine confusion, and apologises half-jokingly if he overdid it.

originalCard.background: Jolene grew up in a Bedok flat where her mother ran a small clothing stall and gave firm opinions on everything, including what Jolene should wear and eat. Jolene absorbed the honesty but not the certainty. After polytechnic, she drifted through warehouse and retail jobs before training as a calibration technician; now she checks weighing scales at a fish market, where vendors argue with her about a fifty-gram discrepancy and she calmly shows them the printout. Her work taught her that numbers can be verified but preferences cannot, and that distinction quietly shaped how she talks. She enjoys her friends, her weekend marketing rounds, and being asked for opinions—provided nobody expects her opinion to be a warranty.

originalCard.personality: Jolene is direct about her own tastes—she'll tell you plainly that she hates a hawker stall or loves a particular kopi—but oddly careful when asked to recommend things to others. Her instinct is to hedge: 'this is just what I like, I can't speak for you.' It's not insecurity; she simply refuses to let personal preference masquerade as an objective guarantee. Once someone says 'I just want a reference, not a promise,' she opens up completely and gives opinions with real conviction. She finds her own hedging slightly embarrassing but does it anyway.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: On London's South Bank, Elliot Shaw has already walked the same short stretch three times, checking a notebook. He starts to turn near you, then stops.
beats.chinese: 在伦敦泰晤士河南岸，Elliot Shaw已经对照笔记本，把同一小段步道走了三遍。他在你附近准备转身，又停了下来。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Excuse me. I was about to turn across here.
beats.chinese: 不好意思。我正准备从这里转过去。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: He steps aside under the trees, leaving the continuous walking space clear. His notebook stays open.
beats.chinese: 他往树下让了让，留出连续通行的空间，手里的笔记本仍然摊着。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Go ahead. I can manage a fourth check in a minute.
beats.chinese: 你先请。第四遍检查晚一分钟也行。

choices.english: A fourth check? What are you checking?
choices.chinese: 第四遍？你在检查什么？

choices.english: Thanks. I'm stopping here. Go ahead.
choices.chinese: 谢谢。我就在这里停一会儿。你先走吧。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: Elliot keeps to the side and turns his notebook towards himself.
beats.chinese: Elliot留在步道一侧，把笔记本转向自己。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: I'm a bus accessibility route surveyor. The walking part matters too. A bus can be easy to board and hard to reach.
beats.chinese: 我做公交线路无障碍勘察。步行这一段也很重要。公交车可能容易上，却不好走到。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: He runs a finger down three matching entries, then readies his pencil over a fourth line.
beats.chinese: 他用手指顺着三条相同的记录划下来，又把铅笔停在第四行上。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Three checks agree. I want one more before I put the notebook away.
beats.chinese: 三遍结果一致。我还想再走一遍，然后才收本子。

choices.english: I'll leave you to it. Goodbye. [Continue along the path.]
choices.chinese: 那就不打扰你了。再见。[沿步道继续走。]

choices.english: Could you show me some local sights while you check?
choices.chinese: 你检查的时候，能顺便带我看看附近的景点吗？

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: Elliot walks the short stretch again without crossing your space. He counts quietly, then stops to write.
beats.chinese: Elliot又走了一遍那段短路，没有穿过你站的位置。他低声数着，随后停下记录。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Same result. That should do it.
beats.chinese: 结果一样。这下该够了。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: He closes the notebook, opens it once to check the page, then catches himself and shuts it again.
beats.chinese: 他合上笔记本，又打开确认了一眼，随即意识到自己的动作，再次把它合上。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: I've got a bus joke. The punchline is delayed. Heh. Two out of ten.
beats.chinese: 我有个公交车笑话。包袱还在晚点。哈。十分里给两分。

choices.english: Goodbye, Elliot. [Continue along the path.]
choices.chinese: 再见，Elliot。[沿步道继续走。]

choices.english: Do you collect jokes like that?
choices.chinese: 你会收集这种笑话吗？

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: You continue along the path. Elliot waits until there is clear space before starting his fourth pass.
beats.chinese: 你沿步道继续走。Elliot等通行空间空出来，才开始走第四遍。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Thanks. Goodbye.
beats.chinese: 谢谢。再见。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: He covers the short stretch, makes one final mark and puts the pencil inside the notebook.
beats.chinese: 他走完那一小段，记下最后一笔，把铅笔夹进笔记本。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Four. Enough.
beats.chinese: 四遍。够了。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: Elliot lowers his pencil and gives a small shake of his head.
beats.chinese: Elliot放低铅笔，轻轻摇了摇头。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: No tours, sorry. I need to watch the path while I work.
beats.chinese: 抱歉，不带游览。我工作时得留意路面。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: He adds the date to his notes and turns towards the section he is checking, keeping the walking space clear.
beats.chinese: 他在笔记上补了日期，转向正在检查的那段路，没有占住通行空间。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: I'll get back to this. Enjoy the river.
beats.chinese: 我接着忙了。好好看看河吧。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: You continue along the path. Elliot lifts his closed notebook in farewell.
beats.chinese: 你沿着步道继续走。Elliot举了举合上的笔记本，向你道别。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Bye. Thanks for the space.
beats.chinese: 再见。谢谢你让出地方。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: He slips the notebook into his jacket pocket and stays under the trees for a moment, looking towards the river.
beats.chinese: 他把笔记本塞进夹克口袋，在树下停了一会儿，望向河面。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Right. Check finished.
beats.chinese: 好了。检查完了。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: Elliot takes out his pencil again, this time opening the notebook at the back.
beats.chinese: Elliot又拿出铅笔，这次把笔记本翻到了后面。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Bad ones, yes. Good ones get enough attention. I've got several about jam. I make that too.
beats.chinese: 冷笑话，会收集。好笑话已经够受欢迎了。我还有几个果酱笑话。果酱我也做。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: He writes a few words on the back page, pockets the pencil and closes the notebook firmly.
beats.chinese: 他在最后一页写了几个词，收起铅笔，把笔记本合严。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: That's the whole collection for this afternoon. I'll leave you in peace. Bye.
beats.chinese: 今天下午就展示这些了。不打扰你了。再见。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: On the South Bank, Elliot stands under the trees, clear of the walking space, holding a wrapped sandwich. He recognises you and lifts his free hand.
beats.chinese: 在泰晤士河南岸，Elliot站在树下不挡路的地方，拿着用纸包着的三明治。他认出你，抬起空着的那只手。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Hello again. Homemade blackberry jam today. Made it myself.
beats.chinese: 又见面了。今天带的是自制黑莓果酱。我自己做的。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: He slowly finishes a mouthful and gathers the wrapper around the sandwich. He doesn't bring up work.
beats.chinese: 他慢慢吃完一口，把三明治外的包装纸拢好，没有提工作的事。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: This lunch break's mine today. Good to see you.
beats.chinese: 今天这点午休归我。见到你真好。

causality.presenceReason: Elliot在用户出现前已为公交线路的步行接驳部分勘察同一小段步道，连续核对三遍。

stories.titleZh: 旧时刻表，多出来的十八分钟

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: On London's South Bank, Victor Lane stands beside the Thames Path with an old ferry timetable. Out for a river walk, he has stopped to read the departures he once coordinated.
beats.chinese: 在伦敦泰晤士河南岸，Victor Lane拿着一张旧渡轮时刻表，站在步道边。他原本出来沿河散步，停下来读起了自己从前调度过的班次。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Ten twelve, ten sixteen... Oh, sorry. Reading aloud. I'm Victor Lane.
beats.chinese: 十点十二分，十点十六分……哦，抱歉，念出声了。我叫Victor Lane。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: He lowers the timetable and moves a little farther to the side, leaving the path clear.
beats.chinese: 他放低时刻表，往旁边挪了一点，让步道保持畅通。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Thirty-one years dispatching ferries. I've got a short story about one of these departures, if you fancy it.
beats.chinese: 干了三十一年的渡轮调度。这上面有一班船，我有个小故事，你要是想听的话。

choices.english: All right. One short ferry story.
choices.chinese: 好啊，听一个简短的渡轮故事。

choices.english: No story for me, thanks. Enjoy your walk.
choices.chinese: 谢谢，我就不听故事了。祝你散步愉快。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: Victor turns the timetable over. There are faded pencil notes on the back.
beats.chinese: Victor把时刻表翻过来，背面留着已经褪色的铅笔笔记。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: One ferry. Fifty passengers. A missing captain. I was twenty minutes behind before we'd even started.
beats.chinese: 一艘渡轮，五十名乘客，船长不见了。还没出发，我就已经晚了二十分钟。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: He raises a finger to continue, then notices a note and brings the paper closer to his glasses.
beats.chinese: 他竖起一根手指，正要往下讲，忽然注意到一条笔记，把纸凑近眼镜。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Here's the honest bit. Twelve passengers. The captain was buying tea. Hang on, the delay's written down here somewhere.
beats.chinese: 说实话，是十二名乘客。船长买茶去了。等等，延误了多久，这里应该记着呢。

choices.english: Go on. What actually caused the delay?
choices.chinese: 继续吧。到底是什么耽误了发船？

choices.english: I'll stop there, thanks. Enjoy the rest of your walk.
choices.chinese: 我就听到这里吧，谢谢。祝你接下来散步愉快。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: Victor nods and folds the timetable without starting his story.
beats.chinese: Victor点点头，把时刻表折起来，没有开始讲故事。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Of course. Enjoy the river.
beats.chinese: 当然。好好看看河景吧。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: He slips the paper into his cardigan pocket and folds his arms. Half the timetable remains sticking out.
beats.chinese: 他把纸塞进开衫口袋，抱起双臂。半张时刻表还露在外面。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: A little more walking for me, then a costume sleeve to mend at home.
beats.chinese: 我再走一会儿，回家还得补一只戏服袖子。

choices.english: Take care, Victor. [Continue along the path.]
choices.chinese: 保重，Victor。[沿步道继续走。]

choices.english: Your timetable's hanging out of your pocket.
choices.chinese: 你的时刻表有一半露在口袋外面。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: Victor finds the note and holds the timetable steady with both hands.
beats.chinese: Victor找到了那条笔记，双手拿稳时刻表。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: The captain came back on time. I held the boat for a man at the dock. He was only waiting for his wife.
beats.chinese: 船长准时回来了。我为了码头上的一个男人压着船没发。人家只是在等妻子。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: He taps the pencilled figure, gives a short laugh and stays beside the path to read the remaining notes.
beats.chinese: 他点了点铅笔写下的数字，短短地笑了一声，留在步道边继续看其余的笔记。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Two minutes late. I've added eighteen over the years. Thanks for listening. I'll check the rest before I tell it again.
beats.chinese: 晚了两分钟。这些年让我多讲出了十八分钟。谢谢你听我说。再讲之前，我得把剩下的也核对一下。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: Victor pauses with his finger halfway down the notes, then folds the timetable.
beats.chinese: Victor的手指停在笔记中间，随后把时刻表折好。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Certainly. I did promise a short one, and I've barely got the captain back.
beats.chinese: 当然。我确实说过要讲个短的，结果讲到现在，船长还没回来。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: He puts the paper away, gives a friendly nod and resumes his walk along the clear side of the path.
beats.chinese: 他收好纸，友善地点点头，沿着步道空着的一侧继续散步。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Good afternoon to you. I'll leave the captain to finish his tea.
beats.chinese: 祝你下午愉快。我就让船长把那杯茶喝完吧。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: As you continue along the path, Victor gives a small wave without following.
beats.chinese: 你沿步道继续前行，Victor轻轻挥了挥手，没有跟上来。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: You too. Mind how you go.
beats.chinese: 你也保重。慢走。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: He unfolds his arms, pushes the loose paper fully into his pocket and turns to look across the river.
beats.chinese: 他放下双臂，把露出的纸完全塞进口袋，转身望向河对岸。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Yes, I'll stop here a minute.
beats.chinese: 嗯，我就在这儿停一会儿。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: Victor looks down and catches the timetable against his cardigan.
beats.chinese: Victor低头一看，连忙隔着开衫按住了时刻表。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: So it is. Thank you. That one's survived long enough without me feeding it to the Thames.
beats.chinese: 还真是。谢谢。这张纸保存了这么多年，可不能让我给喂进泰晤士河里。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: He takes it out, folds it smaller and checks that it fits entirely inside the pocket. He stays to smooth down the bent corner.
beats.chinese: 他把纸拿出来，折小一些，确认能完整放进口袋，又留在原地抚平折弯的一角。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: There. Safely away. Thanks again, and enjoy your afternoon.
beats.chinese: 好了，收稳了。再谢一次，祝你下午愉快。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: At London's South Bank, Victor is standing clear of the path beneath the trees. He recognizes you, holding a theatre costume he brought from home. A short section has already been mended.
beats.chinese: 在伦敦泰晤士河南岸，Victor站在树下、不挡路的地方，认出了你。他手里拿着从家带来的戏服，上面已经缝好了一小段。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: Hello again! I'd like to finish these few stitches quietly today. No long stories from me.
beats.chinese: 又见面了！今天想安安静静把这几针收完，就不讲长故事了。

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.english: He draws the thread snug, folds the fabric in his hands and smiles at you.
beats.chinese: 他收紧线头，把衣料折在手中，朝你笑了笑。

beats.speaker: npc
beats.english: I'll let these stitches do the talking today. Good to see you.
beats.chinese: 今天先让这几针说话。见到你真好。

causality.presenceReason: Victor独自来南岸沿河散步，停下翻阅随身带来的旧渡轮时刻表，回顾自己曾调度的班次。

causality.currentGoal: 原本想散步并看看旧班次，意外念出声后，顺势询问对方是否愿意听一个短故事。
causality.currentState: 今天精神不错、愿意聊天，容易把故事讲长，但对不想听的人仍然客气。
causality.contactTrigger: 他在用户近旁把旧发船时间念出了声，意识到后主动致歉并介绍自己。

结构校验、模型复核与正式编辑批准分别记录；本条保持草稿状态。
2026-11-22 逐人重写 28 处地点的 101 篇双语初遇及重逢，核对人物卡、站位、四路选择和本地口语。
